terms.definition: Relative sparse-leg contribution in weighted fusion: fusion.sparse_weight defaults to 0.3, range 0.0 to 1.0. The fusion code normalizes all three positive weights by their sum at query time, then adds vector, sparse and graph weighted scores per chunk; optional score normalization applies separately to each leg. This weight is ignored in RRF mode, where rank positions drive fusion. Raising sparse weight can favor lexical matches when they rank well, but does not create missing candidates. Keep the model and corpus fixed and compare identifier-heavy and conceptual questions before choosing a balance.

Sets the contribution of BM25-style lexical scoring in hybrid/tri-brid ranking. Higher sparse weight favors exact token overlap (identifiers, symbols, stack traces), while lower values favor semantic similarity from dense vectors. There is no universal best value: the right point depends on corpus cleanliness, query style, and how strong your reranker is. Treat this as a balance knob between precision on exact terms and semantic recall on paraphrased intent, and tune it jointly with sparse top-k and dense candidate counts.

terms.definition: Controls how much timestamp recency boosts Recall candidates relative to semantic similarity. At low values, Recall selects the most semantically similar historical snippets regardless of age; at higher values, newer snippets are favored even if semantic match is slightly weaker. This is a ranking tradeoff, not a retrieval count control. For stable behavior, calibrate recency weighting against conversation length and topic volatility: longer, multi-topic chats usually benefit from moderate recency bias, while short technical debugging threads often need stronger similarity dominance. Evaluate with turn-level attribution checks to confirm selected memories actually support the final answer rather than merely being recent.

terms.definition: Sets how many Recall snippets are passed in standard mode after ranking. This parameter affects both quality and latency: larger top_k improves coverage for multi-part follow-ups but increases token usage and the chance of introducing weakly relevant memory. Smaller top_k is faster and cleaner, but can drop critical constraints from earlier turns. Treat top_k as a task-shape parameter, not a global maximum: narrow troubleshooting flows often perform best with small top_k, while planning or design conversations may need larger values. Pair this with recency weighting and deduplication to prevent near-duplicate memories from consuming context window budget.

terms.definition: Defines how long the system waits for a streaming response before aborting. This is a reliability safeguard against stalled model calls, network interruptions, or overloaded inference backends. Set it too low and valid long-form answers will be cut off; set it too high and failed requests tie up resources and degrade user experience. A practical approach is to align timeout values with observed p95 or p99 completion times for your largest retrieval contexts, then add retry logic and clear UI messaging for partial or timed-out outputs.

Enables incremental token streaming in chat instead of waiting for a fully buffered response. This typically improves perceived responsiveness (faster first-token time) and helps users detect answer direction early, but it requires robust partial-state handling, cancellation logic, and transport fallback when providers or proxies drop streams. Keep it enabled for interactive workflows unless infrastructure reliability is poor; when disabled, ensure the UI clearly indicates buffered mode so users do not interpret waiting as failure.

The current retrieval implementation has no consumer that reads this path for query expansion, so editing it does not currently load a dictionary or change searches. A vocabulary file should be reviewed for ambiguous terms and versioned when a consumer is implemented. For present runs, inspect the actual query and retrieved evidence rather than assuming the file was applied.

File path to the semantic synonym dictionary used during query expansion. The file should be versioned with your project and treated as retrieval configuration, not random text: entries should map domain terms to controlled alternatives (aliases, acronyms, team-specific jargon, and legacy naming). A good synonyms file raises recall by helping sparse and dense retrieval find conceptually equivalent language, but an overly broad file can introduce drift by matching loosely related terms. Keep the file schema consistent, validate JSON on load, and review changes with relevance tests so newly added synonym sets do not silently degrade precision.

terms.definition: Used when no retrieval context is attached and the model must answer directly from user input plus baseline instructions. This prompt should strongly enforce uncertainty handling (ask clarifying questions, avoid fabricated specifics) because there is no external grounding context. It is the best place to define fallbacks for missing details and expected response framing for general questions. Keep direct-mode policies separate from retrieval-mode instructions to avoid references to nonexistent context blocks. During tuning, compare direct-mode helpfulness against hallucination rate and clarification frequency to ensure the model remains useful without overcommitting.

terms.definition: Used when both repository retrieval (RAG) and chat memory (Recall) are attached, so the prompt must define priority and merge rules between two context channels. A robust pattern is hierarchical trust: prefer current retrieved artifacts for factual grounding, then use Recall for user preferences, unresolved decisions, and conversational continuity. Without explicit precedence rules, models often blend channels inconsistently, causing subtle contradictions. This prompt should also instruct the model to surface conflicts when Recall and retrieved documents disagree. Tune with multi-turn regression suites that include changed files, shifted requirements, and stale historical assumptions.

terms.definition: Applied when retrieved corpus snippets are present and should be treated as primary evidence. This prompt should explicitly require grounding behavior: cite or reference retrieved content, prefer provided context over prior assumptions, and acknowledge when context is incomplete. In practice, this mode is where you define conflict resolution rules (for example, newest file snapshot overrides stale assumptions). Keep instructions deterministic so answers remain stable when retrieval order changes slightly. Evaluate with grounded answer rate, citation accuracy, and contradiction checks against retrieved chunks.

terms.definition: Used when conversational memory snippets are present without repository retrieval. This prompt should define how to use memory safely: incorporate relevant prior decisions, preserve user preferences, and avoid treating old assumptions as immutable facts. Because Recall often contains stale or superseded statements, instructions should require temporal caution and conflict checks against the current user turn. In production, this mode benefits from stricter relevance thresholds and explicit refusal to overfit on weakly related memories. Evaluate with long-session benchmarks where user goals evolve over time.

Because these prompts influence multiple downstream components, changes here can silently shift answer grounding quality, citation behavior, and even token cost. Tune this against your model context window, overlap policy, and observed answer grounding rate. In production, treat token target as a measurable retrieval parameter, not a static constant, and retest after model or tokenizer changes.

terms.definition: This temperature is used for direct chat turns with no retrieval context attached. Because retrieval already constrains the answer space, temperature should usually be tuned lower than direct-chat settings to reduce drift from grounded evidence. Higher values can improve phrasing diversity, but they also increase the chance the model over-generalizes beyond retrieved passages. A practical workflow is to tune this jointly with retrieval thresholds: if context precision is high, modest temperature increases can help fluency; if retrieval is noisy, lower temperature prevents compounding errors. Evaluate with groundedness checks, citation adherence, and contradiction rate against source chunks, not only user preference scores.

terms.definition: TEMPO_BASE_URL is the trace lookup base used for deep-linking canonical request traces into Tempo or Grafana Explore. Set it to a URL operators can actually open from the workbench so trace ids become actionable drilldown links instead of inert metadata.

Stored token-budget intent for extended thinking, constrained to 1000–100000. No current generation request consumer applies this UI field. Raising it does not allocate more reasoning tokens, increase model capability or enable thinking output. Use the implemented model/provider controls and inspect actual request metadata before attributing reasoning behavior to it. Schema default: 10000.

Stable conversation identifier used to bind requests to one persistent dialogue state. Reusing the same `THREAD_ID` allows checkpoints, tool outputs, and prior turns to be recovered across retries and restarts; changing it creates a clean session boundary. In multi-user systems, construct IDs deterministically (workspace + user + session) to prevent cross-user context bleed. Treat this value as state-routing infrastructure, not just a label, because it determines where memory is read and written.

terms.definition: Defines the exact tiktoken vocabulary/merge table used to count and split tokens (for example `o200k_base`). The encoding choice must match the target model family; otherwise token budgets, chunk boundaries, and truncation guards can be wrong even when chunk-size settings look correct. Explicitly pinning encoding improves reproducibility across deployments and helps avoid silent fallback behavior. For mixed-model systems, store encoding per model assignment rather than globally.

OpenAI Cookbook: Count tokens with tiktoken

terms.definition: When enabled, token counts are approximated instead of computed with the exact tokenizer. This speeds large indexing passes and quick planning runs, but estimates can drift on code, mixed-language text, and Unicode-heavy corpora where token boundaries are irregular. Use this mode for rough budgeting and capacity checks, then switch to exact counting before final chunking and cost-sensitive production runs. The key tradeoff is throughput versus boundary accuracy.

OpenAI Cookbook: Count tokens with tiktoken

terms.definition: Lowercases text before tokenization to reduce vocabulary sparsity and make matching less case-sensitive. This often improves recall for noisy user queries, but it can also erase meaning in case-sensitive domains (identifiers, product SKUs, legal names, biomedical symbols). For code retrieval and logs, keeping case is usually safer; for broad natural-language corpora, lowercasing may stabilize indexing. Evaluate it with representative queries rather than enabling globally by default.

Applies Unicode normalization (commonly NFKC) before tokenization so visually similar or canonically equivalent forms collapse to consistent code points. This reduces hard-to-debug token drift caused by mixed sources (PDF extraction, OCR, copied web text, multilingual content). It improves index consistency and duplicate detection, but can alter some script-specific distinctions, so validate on domain text before enforcing globally. In practice, normalization is a high-leverage cleanup step for heterogeneous corpora.

links.text: PRAcTICaL: Prompt Compression with Character-Level Merging (arXiv 2025)

terms.definition: Chooses which tokenizer engine drives token-aware chunking and cost/context calculations (for example `tiktoken`, `huggingface`, or simpler fallback methods). Different strategies produce different token boundaries and counts on the same text, which directly changes chunk sizes, truncation points, and retrieval behavior. Pick the strategy that matches your serving model family to minimize budgeting error and split instability. Standardize one strategy per pipeline stage so evaluation metrics remain comparable across runs.

links.text: Length-MAX: Truncation-Resilient LLM Training for Long Inputs (arXiv 2025)

terms.definition: Stored nucleus-sampling preference, constrained to 0–1. Lower values normally narrow token choices in a consumer that sends top_p, but the current non-chat generation consumer does not pass this field to the gateway. Editing it therefore does not prove a sampling change. Chat temperature and actual provider request parameters govern the implemented path. Schema default: 1.

TOPK_DENSE sets how many semantic candidates are pulled from the dense index before fusion. In practice, this controls the recall ceiling for meaning-based matches: if it is too low, relevant chunks can be dropped before reranking ever sees them; if it is too high, latency and downstream rerank cost grow quickly. Tune it against your corpus distribution and query mix by tracking recall@k, answer grounding rate, and p95 latency together, not in isolation. A common pattern is to increase TOPK_DENSE when user questions are abstract or paraphrased, then counterbalance compute by tightening reranker depth or pruning thresholds later in the pipeline.

links.text: Topo-RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Topology-Aware Retrieval (arXiv 2026)
Qdrant Query Points API (limit and retrieval controls)

terms.definition: TOPK_SPARSE sets how many lexical candidates are retrieved from sparse scoring (BM25-style) before hybrid fusion. This value is critical for exact-match behavior such as identifiers, SKU-like tokens, config names, and error strings that dense embeddings can blur. If TOPK_SPARSE is too low, precision may look good while recall silently collapses on keyword-heavy workloads; if too high, you can over-admit noisy boilerplate and increase rerank pressure. Evaluate it jointly with tokenizer configuration and fusion weights so sparse evidence remains a strong but not dominant signal.

links.text: Hybrid Retrieval for Multilingual RAG Systems (arXiv 2025)

terms.definition: Maximum number of local workbench traces retained per corpus, not a duration. More records provide a longer recent investigation history at greater storage and UI cost; fewer discard old evidence sooner. Eviction is count-based in the trace store. External Tempo, Loki and other backends have separate retention configuration. Schema default: 50.

TRACE_SAMPLING_RATE sets the fraction of requests that emit full traces. Higher sampling improves visibility into rare routing failures and latency spikes, but increases telemetry volume, cost, and operator noise. Lower sampling is cheaper but can miss edge cases unless paired with rule-based overrides for errors, timeouts, or high-value tenants. A robust strategy is adaptive sampling: keep a low baseline for normal traffic and automatically raise sampling around deployments, incidents, or anomalous metrics.

links.text: AgentTrace: Comprehensive Tracing for AI Agents (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: TRACING_ENABLED is the master switch for request-level trace capture in the retrieval and generation pipeline. When enabled, each request can emit structured events that explain routing decisions, retrieval candidates, rerank outcomes, and timing breakdowns. This setting is foundational for debugging because it turns opaque failures into inspectable execution paths. In production, keep it enabled with controlled sampling so you retain diagnostic coverage without overwhelming observability storage.

links.text: AgentTrace: Comprehensive Tracing for AI Agents (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: TRACING_MODE selects how request traces are handled in ragweld: local workbench buffering, canonical OpenTelemetry export, OpenTelemetry plus Langfuse generation observability, or fully off. This mode determines which headers and deep links appear in the UI, where spans are emitted, and whether operators can correlate a live request across FastAPI, retrieval, provider routing, and external observability backends. Keep mode changes explicit and test them with live requests so trace continuity, cost attribution, and drilldown links stay trustworthy across environments.

links.text: AgentTrace: Comprehensive Tracing for AI Agents (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Number of training examples processed per optimization step during learning-reranker fine-tuning. Larger batches can improve gradient stability and throughput on strong hardware, but they increase memory pressure and can destabilize local/containerized setups if oversized. Smaller batches are safer for constrained environments and can be paired with gradient accumulation to emulate larger effective batch sizes. Tune batch size together with learning rate and sequence length, since all three interact with convergence speed and overfitting risk.

Defines how many full passes over the reranker training dataset are executed. More epochs can improve fit on stable, representative triplets, but excessive epochs on small or noisy data usually reduce generalization and hurt real query performance. Use held-out validation queries and early stopping signals rather than only training loss to choose this value. As your mined data grows or distribution shifts, retune epochs because the optimal point moves with dataset size and difficulty.

Learning rate for reranker fine-tuning updates. It controls update magnitude and is often the highest-impact training hyperparameter: too high causes unstable loss and catastrophic drift, too low undertrains and wastes epochs. Choose LR jointly with batch size, adapter rank, and warmup schedule, and validate using ranking metrics rather than loss alone. For reranker adaptation, conservative starting values with short sweeps are usually safer than aggressive defaults.

`RERANKER_TRAIN_MAXLEN` sets the tokenizer-level cap used when building reranker training pairs, so every query-document pair is truncated to this maximum length before it reaches the cross-encoder. In implementation terms, this is one of the strongest memory controls in the training loop because self-attention cost grows roughly with sequence length squared; increasing this value can quickly push GPU/MLX memory over the limit and trigger OOM exits. In practice, treat this as a budget knob: start lower for stability, then raise only if error analysis shows that relevant evidence is being cut off and ranking quality is bottlenecked by truncation rather than model capacity.

links.text: BAR-RAG: Boundary-Aware Adaptive Retrieval for Better Reranking (arXiv)

terms.definition: TRIBRID_FUSION configures how dense, sparse, and graph-derived candidates are combined before final reranking. The fusion method (for example weighted sum vs. rank fusion) controls whether the system favors consensus across signals or aggressively promotes a single strong channel. Strong fusion design is workload-dependent: code and identifier-heavy corpora often need lexical strength, while conceptual QA benefits from semantic breadth and graph context expansion. Tune fusion with held-out query sets and monitor per-signal contribution so failures can be traced to the responsible retrieval path.

links.text: Topo-RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Topology-Aware Retrieval (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Stored triplet-file mining mode, initially replace. It describes persistence behavior, not whether negatives are random, semi-hard or hard. Verify the actual mining consumer and the separate triplets_mine_mode setting before relying on an edit; changing this string does not select a negative-sampling curriculum. Schema default: "replace".

Legacy alias for triplet mining strategy selection (`random`, `semi-hard`, `hard`). This setting controls the difficulty of negative examples used to train the reranker. `random` negatives are fast but often too easy; `hard` negatives maximize discrimination pressure but can inject label noise and instability; `semi-hard` is usually the best production default because it balances signal strength and training robustness. Treat mining mode as a data curriculum parameter and re-evaluate it whenever your corpus changes materially.

links.text: Reranker Optimization via Geodesic Distances on k-NN Manifolds (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Location of the JSONL triplets corpus used to mine and train the reranker. Because this dataset defines supervision quality, the path should point to a durable, versioned artifact rather than an ad hoc local file. Maintain a consistent schema (query, positive, negative, metadata) and track generation provenance so model regressions can be traced back to specific triplet revisions. In practice, good triplet hygiene often improves ranking quality more than additional training steps.

links.text: BiCA: Dense Retrieval with Citation-Aware Hard Negatives (arXiv 2025)
Hugging Face Datasets: Loading Local JSON/JSONL

terms.definition: Legacy alias for TRIBRID_TRIPLETS_PATH. This path points to the dataset that defines graph edges as subject-predicate-object triplets for graph-aware retrieval and relationship expansion. Treat this file as a structured knowledge artifact: normalize identifiers, maintain stable predicates, and enforce schema checks before indexing so graph lookups remain deterministic. If triplets are noisy or inconsistent, graph expansion can amplify errors; if they are clean and domain-specific, they provide high-value context that sparse/dense retrieval can miss. Keep ingestion reproducible and validate that triplet updates improve grounded answer quality on dependency and relationship-heavy queries.

links.text: Neo4j Data Import and ETL Guide

terms.definition: Minimum mined triplets required before training starts. Default: 100. Range: 10-10000. If training skips for insufficient data, mine more triplets or lower this for experimentation.

Controls how newly mined triplets are persisted to disk: `replace` creates a clean dataset for a reproducible training run, while `append` extends an existing corpus for incremental hard-negative collection. Use `replace` when you want strict experiment comparability, fixed train/validation splits, and clear provenance. Use `append` when your retrieval index, query set, or domain vocabulary is evolving and you intentionally want longitudinal data accumulation. In production retraining pipelines, pair this setting with dataset versioning and a run manifest so you can trace exactly which mined triplets entered each reranker checkpoint.

links.text: Reranker Optimization via Geodesic Distances on k-NN Manifolds (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: GUI_DIR is the filesystem path used for public UI assets that both frontend code and backend endpoints depend on, such as model catalogs and generated metadata. In RAG/search deployments, this directory often bridges runtime-generated data with static asset serving, so path correctness directly affects what users can select or inspect in the UI. Keep writes atomic to avoid partial JSON reads by the frontend, and prefer explicit volume mounts in containerized environments. If GUI_DIR differs between build and runtime contexts, you can get stale or missing model lists even though indexing and APIs are healthy. Treat this as deployment configuration that should be consistent across local, staging, and production.

links.text: DS SERVE (2026): Scalable Neural Retrieval Serving

terms.definition: Represents a blocking configuration fault that must be fixed before indexing proceeds, such as embedding dimension mismatch, invalid chunk parameters, missing credentials, or contradictory profile settings. Failing fast here protects index integrity by preventing partially-built or semantically inconsistent artifacts from entering production search. In RAG systems, validation errors are cheaper than silent corruption because bad indexes often look healthy until answer quality drops. Resolve by correcting the source config and rerunning validation, not by bypassing checks. Keep error messages actionable so operators know which field failed, why it failed, and the expected valid range.

links.text: Configuration-First Verification and Validation of Agentic AI

terms.definition: Signals a non-blocking but potentially harmful setting combination, for example oversized chunks, disabled dense retrieval, or weak keyword filters that can reduce relevance quality. Warnings let indexing continue while making tradeoffs explicit, which is useful for exploratory runs and incident recovery. In mature environments, recurring warnings should be promoted into profile-level policies or automated guardrails. Treat warnings as hypotheses about future quality regressions and verify them with retrieval metrics instead of ignoring them. The right workflow is acknowledge, monitor, and either tune or formally accept the risk.

links.text: CRUX: Benchmarking and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in RAG

terms.definition: Selects the storage and query engine used for dense-vector retrieval. In practice, this choice determines how embeddings are indexed, how similarity search is executed, and which operational constraints apply (memory profile, filtering behavior, sharding options, and query latency under load). Switching backends is not just a performance toggle: index build strategy, distance metric defaults, and filtering semantics can differ across systems. Benchmark with representative query mixes and metadata filters, then align backend selection with your production constraints: throughput targets, fault tolerance, and operational tooling.

links.text: Vextra: Scalable and Flexible Dense Retrieval Infrastructure (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Master toggle for the dense semantic leg. When enabled, the query is embedded under the corpus's recorded dense contract and searched against the `text-dense` vectors of the corpus generation in Qdrant (cosine similarity); when disabled, retrieval relies on the sparse and graph legs only. Dense retrieval finds paraphrases and conceptual matches that keyword scoring misses. The leg fails closed with a typed 409 when the embedding configuration no longer matches what the corpus was indexed with.

links.text: Vextra: Scalable and Flexible Dense Retrieval Infrastructure (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Number of dense-vector candidates fetched before fusion and reranking. Top-K is a primary recall/latency lever: increasing it broadens candidate coverage and can rescue relevant passages that would otherwise be missed, but raises search and reranker cost. Too small a Top-K can make downstream reranking ineffective because the right candidates never enter the pool; too large a Top-K can flood reranking with low-value items and slow responses. Tune this jointly with reranker Top-N and fusion weights, and evaluate with recall@k, MRR/NDCG, and p95 latency rather than a single metric.

links.text: Exqutor: Dynamic Retrieval Plans for RAG (arXiv 2025)

terms.definition: Minimum dense-vector score admitted by the vector leg, default 0.0, range 0.0 to 1.0; zero disables this extra filter. Ragweld compares returned dense scores against the floor before fusion. Raising it can remove weak matches but can also discard the best available evidence for a hard question. A similarity score is model and distance dependent, not a calibrated probability that an answer is correct. Tune against reviewed queries after a stable index and model contract, and inspect how many candidates survive before changing other leg weights.

Relative dense-vector contribution in weighted fusion. fusion.vector_weight defaults to 0.4, range 0.0 to 1.0. Weights are stored as entered and normalized by the sum of vector, sparse and graph weights at query time; they need not add to one. In RRF mode these weights are not read. A larger active vector share can help paraphrased queries, but may promote broadly topical passages over exact evidence. Compare reviewed questions and actual leg candidates rather than treating the value as a model-independent quality score.

Relative dense-vector contribution in weighted fusion. fusion.vector_weight defaults to 0.4, range 0.0 to 1.0. Weights are stored as entered and normalized by the sum of vector, sparse and graph weights at query time; they need not add to one. In RRF mode these weights are not read. A larger active vector share can help paraphrased queries, but may promote broadly topical passages over exact evidence. Compare reviewed questions and actual leg candidates rather than treating the value as a model-independent quality score.

Controls whether ranking heuristics prioritize first-party project code or third-party/vendor dependencies when scores are close. In large repos, vendor and framework code can dominate candidate lists simply because it is abundant; this setting counterbalances that effect for tasks where users primarily want answers about their own application logic. Prefer first-party mode for product debugging, architecture discovery, and onboarding into your codebase. Prefer vendor mode only when your query intent is explicitly about dependency internals. Evaluate with intent-labeled queries to confirm the mode aligns with expected navigation behavior.

links.text: SaraCoder: Repository-Aware Code Retrieval at Scale (arXiv 2025)

terms.definition:
Negative score adjustment applied during reranking to chunks detected as third-party or vendored code (for example dependencies under vendor/, node_modules, generated SDKs, or mirrored upstream trees). The parameter is most useful when VENDOR_MODE prefers first-party sources and you want your application logic to outrank framework internals for ambiguous queries.

Treat this as a ranking-bias control, not a hard filter: if the penalty is too large, relevant dependency docs can disappear from top results; if too small, repeated library boilerplate can crowd out business logic. Tune with side-by-side eval sets that include both product-code questions and dependency troubleshooting questions so recall and precision stay balanced.

links.text: GitHub Linguist: How vendor/generated files are classified

terms.definition:
Enables image input in chat so messages can include visual context in addition to text. With this flag off, image attachments should be blocked or ignored; with it on, the runtime must route requests to a vision-capable model and include the correct media payload format.

Turning vision on changes both quality and cost profiles: image inputs consume additional processing budget, can increase latency, and may require stricter content handling rules. Validate provider/model compatibility and monitor failure modes where text-only fallbacks accidentally run on image-dependent prompts.

links.text: ReMoRa: Advancing Visual Reasoning in MLLMs (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: Operator secret used for authenticated Voyage requests when Voyage is selected for a supported provider route. A valid credential is required for those requests; its absence is a configuration or call failure, not permission to use stale vectors or silently switch providers. Ragweld also checks the indexed corpus dense contract, so changing a provider or model requires a matching reindex. Store the credential in the operator secret environment, keep it out of source and inspect readiness and request errors when diagnosing provider access.

Target vector dimensionality for Voyage embeddings. This value must match both the selected Voyage embedding model output and the configured vector index schema; mismatches typically cause upsert failures or silent search-quality regressions if vectors are transformed incorrectly.

Higher dimensions can improve semantic separation on hard queries, but they also increase index size, memory pressure, and distance-computation cost. Any dimension change is a schema change in practice: create a new collection/index and re-embed content rather than mixing vectors produced under different dimensions.

Selects which Voyage embedding model generates vectors for indexing and retrieval. The model choice determines embedding behavior (for example code bias vs. general text behavior), output dimensionality, and operational cost/latency characteristics, so it directly affects both relevance quality and infra footprint.

Change this deliberately and evaluate with a fixed benchmark query set. Because model changes alter vector semantics, switching models should be treated as a reindex event: regenerate vectors, rebuild the index, and compare recall@k, reranked precision, and p95 latency before promoting to production.

Model identifier used for Voyage second-stage reranking. After initial retrieval returns candidates, the reranker rescoring step estimates query-document relevance more precisely and reorders the shortlist. This usually improves top-result precision, especially for nuanced or code-heavy intent.

The tradeoff is cost and latency per request proportional to candidate volume. Tune reranker usage together with candidate count (top_k before rerank) and timeout budget; too many candidates can overrun latency targets, while too few can starve the reranker of useful alternatives.

links.text: BAR-RAG: Boundary-Aware Adaptive Retrieval and Reranking (arXiv 2026)

terms.definition: `RERANKER_WARMUP_RATIO` defines what fraction of total optimization steps uses a gradual learning-rate ramp before entering the main scheduler phase. In this training stack, warmup protects early updates when the reranker head and backbone are still unstable, reducing gradient spikes and divergence risk that can otherwise corrupt the first checkpoints. Operationally, this value interacts with total step count: short runs need a smaller warmup fraction so useful learning starts early, while longer runs can tolerate a larger warmup to improve stability. Tune it together with batch size and base LR, because warmup that is too short can destabilize training, while warmup that is too long can waste compute on underpowered updates.

links.text: Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates in Language Model Pre-Training (arXiv)

terms.definition: Runs Ragas generation-quality scoring during eval runs. Each dataset question is answered through the LiteLLM gateway with the retrieved context, then Ragas judges faithfulness and answer relevancy using the configured judge alias and the local embedding model. When enabled, an unavailable judge, missing ragas package, or non-local embedding provider fails the run closed instead of skipping silently.

LiteLLM alias used as the Ragas judge for faithfulness and answer relevancy. Leave empty to use the chat default alias. The alias must be exposed by the authenticated gateway; the eval run refuses to start otherwise.

Ragas metrics computed per eval entry. Supported: faithfulness (claims grounded in retrieved context) and answer_relevancy (embedding similarity between the question and questions regenerated from the answer). Per-entry scores and run means are persisted on the eval run.

Per-request timeout in seconds for Ragas judge calls routed through LiteLLM. Ragas makes several judge calls per entry (claim extraction, NLI verdicts, question regeneration), and local CPU vLLM serving can take minutes per call, so this is deliberately generous. When a judge call exceeds it, the eval run fails closed with a typed 503 instead of silently dropping scores.

LiteLLM alias that grades Promptfoo llm-rubric assertions during a regression run. Leave empty to use the chat default alias. The grader must be exposed by the authenticated gateway; the run refuses to start otherwise and never reports fabricated pass/fail counts.

The application-visible name of one generation route through the LiteLLM gateway. Every GEN row in data/models.json carries a gateway_alias (for example openai.gpt-6-luna, derived from the OpenRouter id openai/gpt-6-luna by replacing / and : with .) and a gateway_upstream (the LiteLLM litellm_params.model, such as openrouter/openai/gpt-6-luna or openai/ragweld-local for the self-hosted vLLM path). infra/litellm-config.yaml is generated from those rows, so the gateway serves exactly the catalog and nothing else. Config fields such as chat.litellm.default_model, generation.gen_model and graph_indexing.semantic_kg_llm_model hold an alias, and a per-request override is written litellm:<alias>. Aliases never contain / or :, so a direct provider identifier can never be mistaken for a gateway route.

The Synthetic Lab's only generation provider, grounded_qa. For selected indexed source excerpts, the generator model is called through LiteLLM to create question/answer rows with an evidence quote. Each row must validate and its quote must match the source under the provider's normalization rules; with curation enabled, System One independently checks whether a real reader would ask the question and whether the evidence supports its answer. Generator or judge failures fail the run. Inspect generated, malformed, ungrounded, judged and kept counts to see where candidates are lost. Chunk-summary and keyword recipes derive deterministic artifacts instead of asking the generator for eval rows.

Reranker training triplets mined from a persisted eval run's retrieval results instead of from directory layout or feedback alone. Each eval entry is a real retrieval trace: its labelled expected paths become positives and the highest-ranked retrieved documents that are not expected become hard negatives, up to learning_reranker_negative_ratio per question. Synthetic triplets/full_stack runs mine the quality-gate retrieval pass this way, and POST /api/reranker/mine adds the corpus' latest eval run (or an explicit eval_run_id) to the feedback-event triplets. Rows carry a source field naming the eval run so lineage stays inspectable.

How many generator/judge requests a synthetic run sends to the LiteLLM gateway at once (synthetic.generator.concurrency). Paid upstream aliases can absorb several parallel requests, which shortens a 200-row run considerably; the local single-stream vLLM serving alias is serialized process-wide (one request at a time across every run in the API process), so two corpora generating concurrently still never queue the local engine against itself.

Output token budget for the eval judges: the Ragas judge alias and the Promptfoo llm-rubric grader (evaluation.judge_max_tokens, default 4096). It is deliberately separate from chat.max_tokens: faithfulness scoring emits statement lists and reasoning-capable gateway aliases spend tokens before the verdict, so a chat-sized cap truncates the judge and the eval run fails closed with LLMDidNotFinishException instead of producing scores. Raise it when judges time out on length; lower it to bound cost on large datasets.

MIMIR_BASE_URL points ragweld at the Grafana Mimir deployment that keeps long-range metrics. Prometheus forwards every sample it ingests to Mimir over remote write, so Mimir answers PromQL for retention windows Prometheus itself no longer holds. Readiness is probed at /ready; when the URL is empty the component reports disabled, never healthy.

PROMETHEUS_BASE_URL points ragweld at the Prometheus server that scrapes the API, gateway, local model and exporters and forwards every sample to Mimir over remote write. Prometheus also evaluates infra/prometheus-rules.yml, so this URL is where the Monitoring surface reads the live alert rules (state, severity, expression, for-duration) and where the Open Prometheus link lands. When the URL is empty the alert-rule feed reports unconfigured instead of showing an empty rule list.

PYROSCOPE_BASE_URL points ragweld at the Grafana Pyroscope server used for continuous profiling. When set, the host API attaches the Pyroscope agent at startup and pushes ragweld-api CPU profiles; the component status reports both server readiness (/ready) and the truthful host-agent state. Empty means profiling is off and the component reports disabled.

FARO_BASE_URL is the frontend RUM collector endpoint (the Alloy faro.receiver /collect URL). When set, the workbench initializes the Faro Web SDK on boot and ships browser errors, web vitals, and session events; Alloy labels them service_name=ragweld-web and forwards logs to Loki. The status probe treats an HTTP 405/415 to GET as listener-present because the intake is POST-only.

ALERTMANAGER_BASE_URL points ragweld at the Prometheus Alertmanager that receives alert rules fired by Prometheus (infra/prometheus-rules.yml). The always-firing RagweldWatchdog alert proves the delivery pipe end to end; its absence from Alertmanager means rule evaluation or routing is broken. Readiness is probed at /-/ready.

GENERATION_RETENTION_SECONDS is how long a replaced index generation (its Qdrant collection and Neo4j graph) stays readable after a promotion before the next commit retires it. Promotion writes a new generation manifest in one Postgres transaction; a request that resolved the old manifest just before that commit still queries the old stores, so the grace must cover the longest request lifetime. A value of 0 retires the replaced generation at the very next commit. Retired generations are dropped by exact id, never by name prefix.

INDEX_RUN_LEASE_SECONDS is the lease on the durable per-corpus index-run fence stored on the corpus row. A running index heartbeats the fence at a tenth of the lease; a second run on the same corpus is refused with a typed 409 while the fence is fresh. A fence whose last heartbeat is older than the lease is treated as a crashed worker: a new run may take it over, and stopping the corpus releases it. Set it longer than the longest pause a run can have without heartbeating.

The evidence panel that opens when you click a citation. It shows the actual cited file rather than a path: a PDF page rendered by the server with the chunk's layout regions boxed, a text or code file scrolled to the cited lines, or the Docling markdown for docx/pptx/xlsx/html with the cited span marked. The viewer only serves files the corpus has indexed and reports when the file on disk has changed since indexing.

Typed record on every chunk of how its text was extracted (direct read or Docling) and, for Docling PDFs, which pages and normalized layout regions the text came from. Captured at index time from Docling's per-item page and bounding-box data; corpora indexed before capture report the state as not captured until re-indexed.

PDF page raster scale used by the source viewer, constrained to 1–4. One unit is 72 dpi, so scale 2 gives 144 dpi. Higher scales improve small text readability but increase rendering work and bandwidth. It affects viewed page images rather than OCR, extraction or the stored document. Schema default: 2.

PDF citation-thumbnail raster scale, constrained to 0.25–1. A small scale keeps chat citations compact; a larger one makes page context clearer but costs additional render work and transfer. It does not change the full-page viewer scale or captured citation regions. Schema default: 0.5.

Maximum text/code file size the source viewer will serve in full, constrained to 65536–50000000 bytes. Larger files produce a typed 413 rather than flooding the browser. Raise it only when large source files are necessary for evidence inspection; doing so increases transfer and browser memory. It does not change indexing limits or PDF rendering. Schema default: 5000000.

Turns on figure/chart/drawing description during indexing for this corpus. Docling detects picture regions on each page, optionally classifies them, and sends each one to the configured vision alias; the description becomes a retrievable chunk anchored to the figure's page and bounding box so citations can box it in the viewer. Off by default because it spends vision calls; the index estimate shows the cost before a run. The run summary reports described / failed (vision call returned nothing) / undescribed (never attempted) counts.

Whether each detected figure is sent to the vision alias for a structured description (summary, labels, components, connections, values, references). Turn off to keep only captions and classification.
Runs Docling's local figure classifier before description so logos, signatures and icons can be skipped and the figure kind (chart, diagram, photo) is recorded on the chunk.

Gateway alias that describes figures at index time. Must be a catalog alias flagged as vision-capable; the run refuses to start otherwise. Defaults to the cheap GLM 5.3 Flash alias; point hard scanned schematics at a stronger vision model per corpus.

Prompt template for figure descriptions. 'technical_figure' covers charts, diagrams and photos in reports; 'schematic' adds drawing number, sheet, revision, connector and unit conventions for engineering drawings.
Raster scale Docling uses for figure crops sent to the vision model (1.0 = 72 DPI; 2.0 ≈ 144 DPI). Higher reads small callouts better at higher token cost.
Figures smaller than this fraction of the page area are not described (icons, logos, decorative marks). Applies only when describe is on (the threshold lives on the description step).

Classifier classes that are never described. The skip applies when the classifier's confident (>= 50%) prediction is one of these classes -- e.g. logo, signature, icon -- not when a listed class merely appears somewhere in the classifier's full prediction list. Has no effect unless classify is on.

Output token budget for one figure description, including any reasoning tokens a reasoning model spends before its JSON reply. A reasoning-heavy vision alias can exhaust this budget on its internal reasoning trace before writing any JSON; when that happens the gateway returns content: null and the figure is counted as failed (figures_failed), not described. Defaults to 2500 to leave headroom for the reasoning trace of the default vision alias on real technical figures.
How many vision calls run in parallel while converting one document.
Seconds to wait for one vision call before the figure falls back to caption-only text.

How many readiness probes in a row must fail before an observability component counts as a real incident on the Operator Deck. A single HTTP probe is a noisy signal - a collector restart, a brief stall or a busy container answers 503 and recovers seconds later - so escalating one miss to a critical incident trains operators to ignore the deck. Below the threshold a failing probe is shown as a warning with its last-N probe history; at or above it the component becomes an incident. Surfaces the API cannot probe at all, such as an ingress that redirects off-host to the auth provider, never advance the streak.

terms.definition: Turns the semantic answer cache on. Unlike a key-value cache it matches on embedding similarity, so a paraphrase of an earlier question can be served from the earlier answer without touching retrieval or the generation model. That is where the saving comes from and also where the risk lives: a near-miss match returns an answer grounded in a slightly different question. Leave it off while a corpus is being re-indexed, because entries written against the previous generation stay valid-looking until they expire.

Which half of the cache is active. read_write is the normal steady state. read_only serves existing entries but writes none, which is what you want while validating a config change: the cache stops absorbing answers produced under settings you are still testing. write_only fills the cache without serving from it, useful for warming after an index rebuild before you trust reads.

Upper bound on cached entries before the oldest are evicted. Each entry holds a query embedding plus the stored response, so this is the main lever on the cache's memory footprint. Sizing it far above the number of distinct questions your operators actually ask buys nothing; sizing it below that thrashes and the hit rate collapses without any error to show for it.

Queries shorter than this are neither served from nor written to the cache. Very short strings embed poorly and sit close to each other in vector space, so a two-character query can match almost anything above the similarity threshold. This is the guard against that class of false hit; raise it if you see unrelated answers returned for terse queries.

Cosine similarity a new query must reach against a cached retrieval query before the cached result set is reused. Retrieval tolerates a looser threshold than generation because the operator still sees the returned chunks and can judge them. Lower values raise the hit rate and the chance of serving results for a subtly different question; measure with your own query log rather than tuning by feel.

The same bar for cached generated answers on the answer endpoint. Keep it above the search threshold: a wrong retrieval set is visible to the reader, a wrong prose answer is not. A mismatch here surfaces as a confidently worded answer to a question nobody asked.

The bar for chat turns, normally the strictest of the three. A chat message is interpreted against its conversation, so two textually similar messages in different threads can mean different things; only a very close match should be reused.

How long a cached retrieval result stays servable. The cache does not observe indexing, so this is the real bound on how long a query can be answered from a superseded index generation after a re-index. Set it shorter than your typical indexing interval, or clear the cache as part of the re-index.

Lifetime of a cached generated answer. Answers age worse than retrieval results because they freeze both the retrieved evidence and the model's phrasing of it; a model or prompt change makes every surviving entry stale in a way nothing will flag.
Lifetime of a cached chat completion, normally the shortest of the three, because conversational context moves fastest and a reused turn from an hour ago reads as the assistant losing the thread.

How many preceding messages are folded into the cache key for a chat turn. Zero keys on the latest message alone, which over-matches across unrelated threads. A larger window makes the key more specific and the hit rate lower; it is the direct trade between reuse and answering the right question.

Skips the cache entirely for requests that carry images. The cache key is built from text embeddings, so two requests with identical text and different attachments are indistinguishable to it. Leave this on unless the cache key is extended to cover attachments.

terms.term: Semantic Cache Max Temperature for Write
terms.definition: Answers generated above this sampling temperature are never written to the cache. A high-temperature response is one sample out of many plausible ones, so caching it turns a deliberate choice to vary into a single frozen answer served to everyone. Deterministic and near-deterministic generations are the only ones worth reusing.

Selects the artifacts this run prepares. Eval dataset generates grounded questions and answers; triplets also mines real retrieval results for reranker supervision; chunk summaries and keywords derive deterministic metadata from indexed chunks; retrieval autotune also proposes a config patch. Full stack prepares all of these. Eval-producing recipes run the retrieval quality gate before completion. Start Full Stack overrides the selected recipe for that launch. Choose a narrow recipe when you only need one artifact: full stack can spend more generation and retrieval work, and artifacts still need explicit publication.

Runnable model alias used to turn selected indexed source excerpts into grounded question/answer rows through the LiteLLM gateway. The picker begins empty unless a previously selected model was saved in this browser; start actions require a selection. This model generates rows; System One independently judges them using the configured reader-question and answer-supported thresholds. A more capable generator may produce useful questions from difficult prose, but compare kept grounded rows and cost rather than raw generated counts. Model or judge call failures fail the run.

Upper bound on indexed source chunks selected for a synthetic run, from 10 to 20,000. Synthetic Lab starts at 150; the API request default is 300. Selection interleaves files and spreads positions through each document with a seeded ordering, so a small budget is not simply the first pages of one file. Increasing the cap broadens possible coverage and generation work; it does not guarantee more accepted questions, because malformed, ungrounded and judge-rejected rows are discarded and Max pairs can stop generation earlier. Index the corpus first.

Upper bound on kept question/answer rows returned by generation, from 10 to 50,000. Synthetic Lab starts at 150; the API request default is 200. The generator processes source chunks in concurrent batches and stops after a batch reaches the cap, then trims the kept rows to this limit. It may generate and judge extra rows in that final batch. For example, a target of 150 does not guarantee 150 usable rows when evidence or curation checks reject candidates. Increase source coverage or improve the generator before treating a larger target as a quality improvement.

Number of question/answer candidates requested from each selected source chunk, from 1 to 20. Synthetic Lab starts at 1; the API request default is 2. Multiple questions can cover different facts within one passage, but they concentrate the dataset on that passage and may repeat the same answer. For broader coverage, try more source chunks before requesting many nearly identical questions from each. Actual kept rows can be lower because evidence matching and System One curation run after generation, and the total Max pairs cap still applies.

Retrieves a run's generated eval questions against the active corpus and checks top-1 accuracy against synthetic.quality_gate.top1_min. The default threshold is 0.40 over up to the first 50 generated entries; entries with expectations that cannot distinguish good retrieval are excluded from scoring, and an empty scored set cannot pass. A failed gate fails an eval-producing run and blocks eval dataset or triplet publication. This is a self-consistency check on generated questions, so even 100% is not external validation. Keep a separately reviewed eval dataset to assess improvements on questions the generator did not create.

Minimum fraction of informative gate questions whose first retrieved result hits the expected file and any required page or line location. Stored at synthetic.quality_gate.top1_min; default 0.40, range 0.0 to 1.0. With 50 informative questions, 20 top-1 hits meet 0.40. Raising this threshold blocks more weak generated datasets; lowering it makes passing easier without improving retrieval. The gate must have at least one informative scored entry even when the threshold is zero. Calibrate it with reviewed questions and stable retrieval settings.

Maximum number of generated eval entries used to decide the synthetic retrieval quality gate. Stored at synthetic.quality_gate.sample_size; default 50, range 1 to 10,000. The gate uses the first entries, bounded by the available dataset, rather than a fresh random sample. A small sample is faster but unstable: with 10 scored entries one hit changes accuracy by 0.10. Triplet and full-stack recipes retrieve all generated entries for mining while the gate still scores its configured subset. Uninformative entries are excluded, so the number actually scored can be smaller than the displayed sample count.

Checks that generated rows are tied to the selected source before they enter an eval artifact. The evidence quote must match source text under the provider's normalization rules, the row must validate, and System One's reader-question and answer-supported probabilities must reach their configured minimums. Generated, malformed, ungrounded, judged and kept counts describe different stages; a large generated count with few kept rows is a quality signal to investigate. Mean cue-word probability is reported for inspection but is not one of the two configured admission thresholds. Grounding checks support inspectability; they do not replace human review of question usefulness or expected answers.

Copies a prepared artifact into the active corpus store for its kind. Eval dataset publication replaces the corpus eval dataset; chunk summaries replace stored summaries; keywords update corpus metadata; triplets replace the configured training file. Eval datasets and triplets require a passed quality gate. Publication records a version and attaches lineage references so the source run remains traceable. Preview the artifact first: publication changes the active destination. Publishing a config patch returns a preview; its separate Apply action writes config. A report is a human-readable file and has no corpus-store Publish action.

Points a corpus lineage alias, such as baseline, canary, current or promoted, at the selected run's captured bundle. The run must be completed, attached to a bundle and free of an explicit failed quality gate; recipes that have no retrieval gate can still promote when completed. The alias identifies a versioned bundle for later comparison and selection. Promotion itself does not publish each artifact into the active corpus store. Review the run's recipe, artifact contents and gate results before changing an alias used as your baseline.

A proposed config change prepared by retrieval-autotune or full-stack recipes from generated expectations and derived keywords. The current recipe uses deterministic adjustments to filename boosts and selected layer bonuses; it does not run a search over configurations or prove that the patch improves held-out retrieval. Publishing this artifact opens its patch preview, and Apply Suggested Config Patch is the separate write. Inspect the exact values, save a baseline and evaluate on reviewed questions after applying. A successful synthetic quality gate evaluates the run's questions, not the proposed config's benefit.

Reasoning budget requested from the selected gateway model during semantic entity and relationship extraction. graph_indexing.semantic_kg_reasoning_effort defaults to medium and accepts minimal, low, medium, high and xhigh; the routing helper translates it to the upstream model's protocol. Greater effort may help difficult relationships but can increase latency and tokens, so compare extraction outcomes and cost on representative documents. This control is independent of schema-proposal reasoning effort. Keep the per-chunk timeout large enough for the chosen model and budget: failed required extraction fails the indexing run.

Maximum eligible chunks admitted to a semantic graph indexing run. graph_indexing.semantic_kg_max_chunks defaults to 40,000, range 1 to 100,000. If the corpus exceeds this ceiling, the run fails before promotion; the indexer does not quietly extract a graph from only the first chunks. This is a work and completeness guard, not a target sample size. For example, a 45,000-chunk corpus needs a ceiling of at least 45,000 or a deliberate corpus/chunking change. Raising it permits more LLM extraction work and should be considered together with the model, estimate and timeout.

Seconds allowed for each semantic graph extraction LLM call through the gateway. graph_indexing.semantic_kg_llm_timeout_s defaults to 90, range 5 to 600. It bounds each request rather than the entire corpus run. A low limit catches stalled calls quickly but can reject valid extraction from a slower model or high reasoning effort. A larger limit allows those calls longer and delays failure detection. The extraction client disables its own retries so one timed-out call does not silently multiply paid work; required extraction failures fail the indexing run.

Weight recorded on code-graph containment edges, such as a module containing a class or function and a class containing a method. graph_indexing.ast_contains_weight defaults to 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0, and applies when the code-graph indexing policy is selected. Lower values label containment edges as weaker relative to other code relationships; they do not change which source symbols the parser discovers. Treat the weight as relationship metadata and verify how your graph retrieval consumes it before assuming that lowering it removes edges. Reindex to write changed edge weights.

Weight recorded on resolved class-to-base-class inheritance edges in the code graph. graph_indexing.ast_inherits_weight defaults to 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0. For example, a resolved ReportGenerator inheriting BaseGenerator gets this weight; unresolved bases are reported rather than invented. Use a lower weight when inheritance should carry weaker evidence than explicit calls or imports, and compare relevant graph queries after reindexing. The setting controls edge metadata, not Python inheritance semantics or whether a base can be resolved.

Weight recorded on module import relationships extracted for the code graph. graph_indexing.ast_imports_weight defaults to 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0. An import establishes a dependency, which can help investigate modules using a shared component, but does not prove that the imported function is called. Lower this relationship's weight when import-heavy modules would otherwise appear too strongly connected in a consumer that uses weights. Reindex to update the stored graph; changing the value does not alter source parsing or execute imported code.

Weight recorded on resolved function, method or class call edges in the code graph. graph_indexing.ast_calls_weight defaults to 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0. Class construction is represented as a call to the class; duplicate calls between the same pair are collapsed, and unresolved calls are reported rather than guessed. This can support dependency questions such as which handler calls a storage function. Lowering the weight weakens relationship metadata for consumers that use it; it is not a runtime call count. Reindex after changing it.

Allows a full replacement index when embedding or sparse settings differ from the corpus's recorded contracts. Indexed corpora normally lock those fields so query vectors match stored vectors. With Force reindex selected, review the estimate and consent to a rebuild; the replacement becomes active after validation. Changed saved settings can make searches unavailable until the matching rebuild succeeds. Use it for a deliberate model, dimension, tokenizer or BM25 contract change, and confirm the completed run and retrieval results afterward. It is not a shortcut around validation or a promise that every document will index successfully.

Chooses who orchestrates a Learning Agent run. The schema default is local: Ragweld executes the workflow in-process. flyte creates a Flyte execution using the configured project, domain and registered launch plan; the task calls this API's execute boundary, and Flyte owns execution status and cancellation. Select flyte only after its readiness checks pass. Missing configuration or an unavailable Flyte service blocks launch with a structured 503; it does not switch to local execution.

Selects local or mlflow run tracking, independently of workflow orchestration and the training engine. The schema default is local. mlflow records run parameters, metrics and artifacts on the configured tracking server under the configured experiment. Use MLflow when operators need a shared experiment history; keep its tracking endpoint reachable from the Ragweld backend. If selected MLflow is unavailable, launch fails with a structured 503 instead of silently tracking locally.

Backend-reachable HTTP base URL for Flyte Admin. Ragweld uses it to check health, resolve the registered launch plan, create executions and control their lifecycle. The schema default is empty; it is required when workflow backend is flyte. Use the address reachable from the Ragweld API process, and configure the separate Console URL for browser links. A reachable server alone is insufficient: the selected project, domain and launch plan must also resolve.

Browser-facing Flyte Console address used for operator links to workflow executions. The schema default is empty. Set an address the operator's browser can reach, which may differ from the private Admin endpoint used by the backend. This field provides navigation; it does not deploy Flyte or establish workflow readiness. Keep it aligned with the Flyte service that owns the configured project and domain.

Project namespace used to resolve the Learning Agent launch plan and own its Flyte executions. The schema default is ragweld. Use the same project used when registering the workflow; changing the name does not create or migrate a project. A mismatch can leave Admin reachable while launch-plan readiness fails. Separate projects can organize independently managed workloads, but their registrations and permissions must match.

Flyte environment namespace within the selected project, used for launch-plan lookup and executions. The schema default is development. Match the domain used during workflow registration, such as development or a separately configured production domain. Changing this field changes where Ragweld looks for registered workflows; it does not provision that environment or copy registrations. Verify readiness after changing project or domain.

Name of the registered Flyte launch plan used to start Learning Agent workflows. The schema default is empty; the UI suggests learning-agent-train. It must resolve in the configured project and domain before a flyte run can launch. Register the matching workflow with the repository's registration script and verify readiness. A launch plan identifies executable workflow configuration; entering a name does not register it or select a different training engine.

Address of this Ragweld API as reachable from Flyte task pods. The workflow task calls the API's execute boundary and follows the training run there. The schema default is empty and flyte launch requires a value. Use a pod-reachable hostname or IP and the actual API port; localhost inside a pod refers to that pod, not the Ragweld API host. This direction of connectivity is separate from Ragweld's outbound connection to Flyte Admin.

Backend-reachable MLflow Tracking server URL for Learning Agent runs. The schema default is http://127.0.0.1:55500. With tracking backend mlflow, Ragweld resolves or creates the selected experiment and records run data through this endpoint. Use the address reachable from the API process; configure the browser Console URL separately when operators use a public hostname. An unreachable selected tracking server blocks launch, so verify readiness before starting a long training run.

Experiment that groups Learning Agent runs on the configured MLflow Tracking server. The schema default is ragweld-learning-agent. Ragweld resolves or creates this experiment before an MLflow-tracked run starts. Keep a stable name to compare related runs; use a different name to organize a distinct experiment series. Renaming this setting routes future runs to another experiment and does not move earlier history.

Container image or artifact reference recorded for the intended Unsloth training lane. The schema default is empty. This identifies an execution artifact, not a GPU allocation or a working trainer. The current Learning Agent start boundary only accepts mlx_qwen3 execution and rejects other engines with a structured unavailable error; filling an image does not enable Unsloth. Treat this as target-lane configuration until a supported CUDA execution path is implemented and verified.

Readable dashboard-name portion of the embedded Grafana URL, paired with its stable dashboard UID. The schema default is on-call-overview. Select a dashboard preset to update both fields together; custom dashboards should use the slug shown by Grafana's dashboard URL. Editing the slug only changes the constructed link and does not rename or provision a dashboard.

Controls whether the Grafana dashboard is displayed inside Ragweld as an iframe. The schema default is enabled. Disable it when operators prefer an external Grafana window or embedding is blocked by the deployment's authentication or frame policy. This changes presentation only: it does not stop telemetry collection or the Grafana service. A working embed still needs a browser-reachable base URL and Grafana configuration that permits framing.

Controls Grafana chrome in the embedded dashboard URL. The schema default is tv; the UI offers None, tv and 1 (minimal). Use tv for a focused wallboard, minimal for reduced chrome, or None when operators need normal Grafana navigation. This affects the dashboard display, not trace sampling, telemetry retention or dashboard queries.

Grafana organization selected by the embedded dashboard URL. The schema default is 1 and the minimum is 1, with no configured upper bound. Match the organization that owns the dashboard and data sources. Changing the number does not create an organization or grant access; an incorrect ID can show missing dashboards or permission errors even when Grafana itself is reachable.

Automatic refresh interval passed to the embedded Grafana dashboard. The schema default is 10s; the UI gives examples 5s, 30s and 1m. Shorter intervals make recent activity visible sooner but cause more dashboard queries. Longer intervals reduce query load and suit historical investigation. This is a display refresh setting, not the application's telemetry collection or scrape interval; Grafana may enforce its own minimum refresh interval.

Selects a named dashboard from Ragweld's configured preset catalog and updates the dashboard UID and slug together. Use a preset for the corresponding operator view, or Custom when entering another provisioned Grafana dashboard manually. The selector chooses which dashboard to open; it does not create dashboards or change the telemetry backend. Confirm the selected UID exists in the configured Grafana organization.

Recent time window shown by the embedded dashboard, from now minus the selected duration through now. The dashboard selector offers 5 minutes through 30 days. Short windows help inspect a specific recent incident; longer windows reveal trends but query more history and can hide brief spikes in aggregated panels. This local view setting changes dashboard queries, not retention or telemetry collection. Combine it with Refresh to control how often the window advances.

OpenCost endpoint used by Ragweld's observability status check and operator link. The schema default is empty, which leaves the component disabled. A configured address is probed at /healthz; entering a URL does not install OpenCost or provide Kubernetes cost data. Configure it only for an existing OpenCost deployment with its required cluster integration, and verify the functional status before relying on cost visibility.

Data-size assumption used by the storage planner, with an explicit binary unit such as MiB or GiB. For an indexed active corpus the planner seeds this from stored chunk-content bytes; otherwise its generic starting value is 5 GiB. Edit it to explore growth scenarios. This is a planning input, not a measured total across databases or the original files on disk, and it does not change corpus configuration.

Average chunk-content size in bytes used to estimate chunk count as ceiling(corpus bytes / chunk bytes). The generic starting value is 4 KiB; an indexed corpus seeds a representative size from live chunk bytes and point count. Smaller values predict more chunks, vectors and storage. This byte-based planning assumption is distinct from token-based indexing settings and does not rechunk the corpus.

Number of numeric values per dense vector in the storage estimate. It is seeded from embedding configuration and may be edited for a what-if scenario. Dense bytes scale linearly with chunk count, dimensions and bytes per value. Use the dimensions of the actual embedding model rather than assuming a vendor-wide size. Changing this planner value does not change the indexed embedding contract or re-embed data.

Bytes per vector value assumed by the planner: float32 uses 4, float16 uses 2 and int8 uses 1. Lower precision reduces the raw-vector estimate; whether it is valid and how it affects retrieval depends on the actual database and quantization configuration. This selector performs size arithmetic only and does not enable quantization. Measure relevance and real memory use before treating a smaller estimate as a deployable configuration.

Multiplier used to estimate the dense-vector index allocation from raw vector bytes. The planner starts at 1.3 and adds the multiplied allocation separately from raw embeddings in its total. This is an approximation rather than measured Qdrant disk use; graph structure, payload indexes, quantization and storage mode can change the real footprint. Calibrate it against representative live collections, and do not interpret the input as a Qdrant HNSW tuning parameter.

Percentage of assumed corpus bytes budgeted as an additional hydration allocation. The generic starting value is 100%, so the estimate adds one corpus-sized allocation. Raising it increases the planning total; lowering it reduces that allowance. This is a capacity assumption, not a control that loads a chosen percentage of Ragweld data into RAM. Compare the estimate with measured database and process memory before sizing a host.

Number of copies assumed for selected storage components in the planner. The generic starting value is 3. The calculation adds replication-factor-minus-one copies of its critical components; its sparse estimate is not included in that replicated subset. Higher values increase capacity estimates but do not configure replicas, failover or availability in Qdrant, Postgres or Neo4j. Match this assumption to the topology you intend to deploy.

Estimated number of Neo4j nodes used by the planner's graph-size arithmetic. The generic starting value is 10,000. The node allocation is node count times average node bytes; the planner also adds a separate approximate index allowance. Use a representative graph count when available and allow for lexical chunks as well as extracted entities. This input does not create nodes or control graph extraction.

Estimated relationship count used by the Neo4j storage planner. The generic starting value is 25,000. More relationships increase the predicted graph allocation even if the node count stays fixed. Use a representative graph's relationship density to estimate growth; extraction strategy and lexical links can produce very different counts. This input only changes the estimate and does not change graph-building behavior.

Average bytes assumed per Neo4j node, including its properties and labels. The generic starting value is 256 bytes; multiplying it by estimated node count gives the planner's node allocation. Larger text properties can make this assumption too small. It is not a measured Neo4j record size or a database storage setting; calibrate it from a graph with similar node contents and include separate index allowance.

Average bytes assumed per Neo4j relationship, including properties. The generic starting value is 128 bytes; multiplying it by relationship count gives the planner's relationship allocation. Rich relationship properties require more space than bare links. This is an estimate rather than an enforced record limit, and changing it has no effect on the stored graph.

Capacity budget against which the compression planner compares its estimated storage scenarios. The generic starting value is 5 GiB. Set the budget for the intended deployment and inspect which assumptions make each scenario fit. This is a planning threshold, not a storage quota or enforcement setting. Reserve additional headroom for temporary indexing generations, backups, logs and growth beyond the components included by the calculator.

Sparse-search storage allowance as a percentage of assumed corpus bytes in the compression planner. The generic starting value is 20%; the main estimator uses a fixed 20% assumption. Increase it if representative sparse vectors and their indexes need more space. It is neither a BM25 relevance weight nor a measured sparse index size, and it does not configure Qdrant storage.

Chunk-summary storage allowance as a percentage of assumed corpus bytes in the compression planner. The generic starting value is 10%; the main estimator uses a fixed 10% assumption. More or longer stored summaries can require a larger allowance. This changes the storage estimate only and does not enable summaries, alter their prompts or control how many are generated.

Maximum retrieval result count requested for this conversation, overriding its corpus's configured final_k. The UI accepts 1–100. Clear the field to restore the corpus default; the override is local conversation state and does not save a new corpus configuration. Higher values can improve coverage but add prompt context and retrieval work; lower values keep context focused. The model's prompt budget can still trim retrieved context.

Requests live public-web grounding for chat turns in this conversation. The UI starts with Web off. The server must also enable chat web search, and the selected gateway alias must be backed by OpenRouter; unsupported routes fail rather than pretending to search. Use Web for current public information and review its citations. This conversation toggle does not change the server's web-search policy or index web pages into a corpus.

Adds prior conversation memory as a selected source using the Recall corpus. Recall is shown separately from ordinary corpora in the source summary. Use it when a turn depends on earlier discussion, and use the adjacent intensity selector to override automatic gating. Selecting Recall is distinct from enabling background conversation indexing; retrieval can only use memory that has been stored. Treat earlier turns as historical context that may have been superseded.

Corpora selected as retrieval sources for the current conversation. The source list refreshes when opened and shows whether each corpus is indexed. Select indexed corpora relevant to the question, then choose which retrieval legs to include. Selection changes the chat request's source IDs; it does not index a corpus or change its saved retrieval settings. Multiple selected corpora broaden the evidence pool and may add retrieval and prompt-context work.

Conversation-level inclusion flags for Vector, Sparse and Graph retrieval over selected corpora. The UI starts with Vector and Sparse on and Graph off. Vector uses semantic embeddings, Sparse uses lexical matching and Graph adds graph-backed retrieval. Turning a leg off excludes it from the request; turning it on still requires compatible indexed data and server configuration. These controls do not rebuild indexes or save new corpus-wide enablement settings.

Dataset-generation recipe to open in Synthetic Lab. Learning Agent Studio offers an eval dataset or eval dataset plus extras; Reranker Studio offers triplets from the current eval dataset or fresh eval plus triplets. Select the recipe appropriate to the trainer's required data shape. This choice prepares navigation to the Lab with that recipe; it does not generate data or start training. Review generator selection and the configured judge before running generation.
