Read-only guidance showing that synthetic dataset generation runs from Synthetic Lab with explicit model selection. Open Synthetic Lab transfers the selected recipe and training context, with automatic execution disabled. Review corpus, recipe and model choices there before starting a generation run. This field is not the training-engine selector or a command input, and opening the Lab does not launch generation or training.

Enables the LiteLLM gateway configuration used for application generation. The schema default is true. Ragweld routes generation through the gateway; disabling it does not select a direct local-model route. Keep it enabled when using chat and verify authenticated gateway readiness. This configuration toggle does not itself start or stop the LiteLLM process.

Backend-reachable OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM API root. The schema default is http://127.0.0.1:54000/v1; generation appends /chat/completions. Use the address reachable by the Ragweld API, including the API-version path, and verify it with the configured client credential. This differs from a browser console URL or a direct local-serving endpoint. A configured address alone does not prove authentication or model availability.

Gateway alias selected as the configured generation default. The schema default is ragweld-local and validation requires a nonempty gateway alias. Enter an alias exposed by the configured gateway and represented in the model catalog, rather than an arbitrary upstream model identifier. Aliases let LiteLLM own provider routing; changing this field does not install a model or rewrite the gateway's alias mapping. Verify readiness and task quality after changing it.

Enables the configured local-serving reference used by Ragweld's serving readiness checks. The schema default is true. vLLM serves behind a LiteLLM alias and is not a direct application generation route. Use this setting to describe the intended serving layer, then verify the process and model actually reported by it. Changing the checkbox does not start or stop the serving process.

OpenAI-compatible endpoint of the expected local-serving layer, used for serving readiness. The schema default is http://127.0.0.1:58080/v1. Keep it aligned with the serving endpoint targeted by LiteLLM's local alias. This is not the application's generation gateway URL: chat requests still route through LiteLLM. Use a backend-reachable address and verify the serving model and context window.

Model identifier Ragweld expects the local-serving endpoint to report. The schema default is mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit. Readiness compares the served model and its context window with this value and the catalog's ragweld-local entry. Enter the actual serving model identifier, not the LiteLLM alias. Editing this reference does not download or load a different model; change the serving deployment and catalog coherently before relying on the new expectation.

Illustrative storage scenario that assumes raw dense vectors occupy one eighth of the float32 baseline. The calculator applies that assumption to its Minimal plan and omits local hydration there; its Low Latency plan assumes float16 and the selected hydration allowance. These are arithmetic estimates, not applied Qdrant configurations or measured latency or relevance results. Product-quantization quality depends on the dataset and actual quantization settings; this calculator establishes no fixed accuracy-loss percentage.

Human-readable name shown for a corpus in source selection and operator views. Choose a name that identifies the collection's content or purpose. The display name is metadata distinct from the stable corpus ID and filesystem path. Editing it in Infrastructure changes the existing corpus's metadata; entering it during corpus creation names the new collection. A name alone does not discover documents or build an index.

Optional explanatory metadata for a corpus. Use it to record the collection's purpose, coverage or intended use so operators can distinguish similarly named corpora. Editing the description does not alter document text, retrieval ranking or the index. In Infrastructure, the Save action also writes database connection settings, so review that action's confirmation before committing metadata changes.

Reference run selected in Run Diff. When two or more runs are available, the view initially selects the second-most-recent run as baseline and the newest as current. Choose a baseline relevant to the change being evaluated; both selectors must name different runs to request a comparison. This view compares recorded runs and does not rerun evaluation or change which adapter is active.

Candidate run compared with the selected baseline in Run Diff. The newest available run is the initial selection. Compare runs with compatible metrics and evaluation conditions so the displayed changes are meaningful. Selection requests a read-only comparison; it does not promote an adapter or start training. For Learning Agent comparisons, metric deltas are current minus baseline, so a negative loss delta indicates lower loss.

Question or search text used to score one query-document pair with the learning reranker's debug endpoint. Enter a representative query and a candidate passage, then run the probe with an active corpus selected. This isolates pair scoring for inspection; it does not perform corpus retrieval, produce a full ranking or train the model. Compare relevant and irrelevant passages for the same query rather than treating one score as an overall quality benchmark.

Candidate passage paired with the query in the learning-reranker score probe. Paste the actual text whose relevance you want to inspect; the probe sends this text rather than fetching a file by path. The configured reranker maximum length bounds model input. This diagnostic does not index the passage or add it to a training dataset.

Requests backend-specific raw yes and no logits along with the pair score when supported. The probe defaults to off, and raw values may be absent even when requested. Logits are unnormalized model outputs useful for debugging scoring behavior; they are not calibrated probabilities or proof of relevance. Enabling this diagnostic output does not change training parameters or the candidate passage.

Local magnification of the training-telemetry projection. The slider ranges from 0.25 to 4 in steps of 0.05, with a starting value of 1. Zoom in to inspect a small section of the trajectory or out to see more of its history. This scales the rendered view and does not change model weights, training steps or the telemetry data. Reset view restores normal zoom and pan.

Keeps the gradient-telemetry view's cursor at the newest available projection point. Live starts enabled. Turn it off to inspect an earlier point without incoming telemetry moving the cursor; turn it back on to follow new data. Pausing the visualization does not pause the training run or stop telemetry collection.

Selects which service logs the chat inspector streams from Loki: API, Postgres, Neo4j, or all three. Changing the filter reconnects the log stream with the corresponding LogQL service selection and the current trace/time context. Use the service associated with the suspected failure to reduce noise, or all to follow a request across dependencies. This filters the displayed logs; it does not change logging levels, request routing or stored logs.

Gateway models selected for a side-by-side benchmark run. The current UI permits 2–4 models and uses aliases discovered through the LiteLLM-backed model list. Choose models that can answer the same task and review grounding, latency and cost together. More selected models create more generation work and potential provider spend. Selecting models here does not change the default chat alias; a benchmark starts only when its run action is used.

Enables graph construction during an operator indexing run for this corpus. graph_indexing.enabled defaults to true. External document corpora use semantic entity and relationship extraction when this is on; selecting Build code graph switches eligible code corpora to parsed code relationships. Runtime-managed internal corpora are excluded by policy. Turning graph indexing off avoids that graph-building work, but is distinct from enabling or disabling the graph search leg. Review the corpus policy and estimated extraction work before indexing: required semantic extraction failures fail the run rather than promoting an incomplete graph.

Stored graph_indexing.build_lexical_graph setting, default true, whose schema describes Document and Chunk nodes linked by NEXT_CHUNK relationships. These lexical links identify document structure and adjacent chunks, as distinct from semantic entities and relationships. In the current indexing implementation this field has no runtime consumer, so changing the checkbox does not establish that lexical graph construction will be enabled or disabled. Use the run's actual graph status and contents to assess what was built; do not use this stored value as proof of graph coverage.

Stored evaluation.eval_multi_m count, default 10, range 1 to 20, presented as Multi Q M (variants) in Eval Analysis. The current evaluation executor does not read this field, so increasing it does not currently create more evaluation query variants. Keep this limitation in mind when comparing runs: a saved value of 10 is not evidence that ten rewrites were executed. Inspect actual retrieval results and query traces to determine which queries ran. The setting needs executor wiring before its advertised variant-count behavior can be measured.

Comma-separated keywords stored on this corpus, such as salinity, calibration, sensor. The Repository Config input trims empty values and saves changes after about one second. Retrieval checks whether any corpus keyword occurs in the lowercased query; when keywords.keywords_boost is greater than 1, that condition applies the configured multiplier to candidate scores. This is a query-level corpus hint, not an exact requirement that each candidate contain the keyword, so it does not necessarily change relative ranking within one corpus. Choose specific vocabulary and inspect recorded boosts; broad words can apply more often than intended.

Corpus metadata shaped as an intent-to-layer-to-multiplier JSON object, for example {"implementation":{"retrieval":1.1}}. Repository Config waits about one second and saves parseable JSON; invalid JSON stays in the editor until corrected. The current retrieval scoring path uses the typed layer_bonus configuration and does not consume this corpus layer_bonuses metadata, so saving this JSON does not currently prove a ranking change. Use the live layer-bonus controls and inspect retrieval score metadata for measurable tuning, and retain this distinction when comparing stored corpus settings.

Maximum entities requested for the current graph view, initially 200, with choices 100, 200, 500, 1,000 and 2,000. Changing Draw at most reloads a bounded subgraph for the active query. It is session view state, not an indexing cap or a persisted retrieval setting: a corpus can contain many more entities than the canvas displays. Larger views reveal more connections but can make the graph slower and harder to read. Use the shown/total counts and search to explore beyond the visible subset; Reset returns the view to its default limit.

Chooses which entity types from the loaded graph are visible in the current view. Types are collected from actual corpus statistics and loaded entities, rather than a fixed list; the legend describes the types currently drawn. All types are selected initially. Clearing a type hides its entities locally and removes their incident edges from the displayed graph, so an empty view can reflect filtering rather than an empty index. These checkboxes do not delete entities, change extraction schemas or configure the graph retrieval leg. Re-enable types to restore the view.

Chooses which relationship types are visible among the loaded graph's entities. The available types come from actual statistics and loaded relationships; all are selected initially. Filtering can isolate calls, containment or a domain relationship while keeping the rest of the corpus intact. It only changes the current display and does not delete edges or change graph search configuration. If entities appear disconnected, check this filter and the entity-type filter before concluding that relationships were not indexed. Re-enable types to restore their visible connections.

Comma-separated file labels that identify relevant retrieval results for one eval question. Matching normalizes slashes and case and accepts a complete path-segment suffix: sensor-calibration.md can match docs/sensor-calibration.md, but mail.txt does not match blackmail.txt. Any matching expected path can count as a hit, with an optional page or line range making the expectation more precise. On a single-document corpus, a whole-file expectation accepts every chunk and is reported as uninformative. Choose the files that actually answer the question and add a location when whole-file labels cannot distinguish good retrieval.

Optional reference answer entered for an eval question. Promptfoo uses this text as the llm-rubric criteria when grading the generated answer; it is not a literal string-equality check. Entries without an expected answer are skipped by that grader. State the facts an acceptable answer must include, such as a calibration interval and its conditions, rather than prescribing unnecessary wording. Expected paths and locations separately label retrieval relevance, so a correct first retrieved file does not by itself prove the generated answer satisfies this rubric. Review model-graded failures and judge consistency.

Number of leading eval dataset entries selected for a Promptfoo regression run. The panel defaults to 25 and offers 10, 25, 50, 100 or the full dataset. Entries in that selected prefix without an expected answer are skipped, so the number actually graded can be lower than the chosen size. Each eligible entry is answered through the gateway and model-graded against its expected-answer rubric; larger runs cost more calls and take longer. This is a prefix selection, not a random representative sample. Use a small run while editing rubrics and a full reviewed dataset when assessing regressions.

Sampling temperature sent to the synthetic question generator. synthetic.generator.temperature defaults to 0.0, range 0.0 to 2.0. A low value favors repeatable phrasing; raising it can diversify candidate questions but can also produce more unsupported or malformed rows. Evidence matching and System One curation still apply, so judge success by kept useful questions rather than diversity alone. For comparisons, hold source selection and other generation limits fixed. The upstream model may restrict supported sampling settings; a rejected request fails generation instead of silently substituting a different value.

Output-token budget for one synthetic generator response. synthetic.generator.max_tokens defaults to 1,200, range 100 to 16,000. It limits the response for a source request, not the total run or the source excerpt length. Asking for many pairs per source can require more space for questions, answers, evidence quotes and JSON structure; too little output room can truncate a response and lose usable rows. Raising the budget permits longer paid output but does not guarantee stronger grounding. Check malformed-row counts and the requested pairs before increasing it.

Maximum characters requested for each generated question. synthetic.generator.question_max_chars defaults to 180, range 50 to 500. The generation prompt includes this limit to keep questions compact and independently understandable. Too tight a limit can remove qualifiers needed to disambiguate a question; too broad a limit permits verbose questions that are harder to review. For example, retain the sensor type or operating condition when two sections discuss different intervals. This is a question-text budget, separate from response tokens, evidence quote length and expected-answer length. The provider also rejects rows exceeding this character limit, so an oversized field is not merely shortened into a kept row.

Maximum characters requested for the evidence quote anchoring a generated row to its source. synthetic.generator.evidence_quote_max_chars defaults to 200, range 50 to 1,000. A compact quote is easier to inspect and match, but it must retain enough text to support the expected answer. A longer quote can include needed conditions at greater output cost. For example, an interval without the sentence identifying which equipment it applies to can be misleading even when copied exactly. Source matching and System One answer-support checks still determine whether the candidate survives. The provider also rejects rows exceeding this character limit, so an oversized field is not merely shortened into a kept row.

Maximum characters requested for the expected answer in a generated eval row. synthetic.generator.expected_answer_max_chars defaults to 400, range 50 to 2,000. Short answers are easier to inspect and use as grading criteria, but must retain essential facts and conditions from the source. Longer answers consume more response space and can introduce claims the quote does not support. Use enough room for the required answer, then inspect evidence and curation outcomes. This limit does not cap the answer later produced by chat or Promptfoo's model under test. The provider also rejects rows exceeding this character limit, so an oversized field is not merely shortened into a kept row.

Maximum lines of a selected source chunk sent as context to the synthetic generator. synthetic.generator.source_excerpt_max_lines defaults to 80, range 10 to 500. This is a per-source line cap, distinct from the number of source chunks selected and from the model's token window. A shorter excerpt reduces input work but can omit facts or qualifiers in a long chunk; a longer excerpt preserves more context while using more input tokens. Questions and evidence must be grounded in the excerpt the generator actually received. If useful answers are repeatedly absent, inspect chunk boundaries and excerpt coverage before increasing pair counts.

Optional gateway alias chosen for this conversation instead of the configured chat gateway default. Choose a model available in the catalog-backed gateway list and suited to the required text, vision or Web capabilities. This local selection does not rewrite the saved default alias or install an upstream model. Image-bearing turns can still use the server's explicit vision-model override, and unsupported provider capabilities fail instead of silently selecting another model.

Task sent to each selected benchmark model so their responses can be compared on the same input. Write a representative question with enough detail to judge answer quality. When a corpus is selected, the benchmark retrieves shared context and gives the same retrieved chunks to the models; inspect grounding status alongside latency and cost. Editing the prompt does not run the benchmark or change the models' system configuration.

Filters the Config Explorer field list by its registered integration, such as the serving, retrieval or observability system a field belongs to. Use it to inspect one integration's settings together. It changes the displayed list only and does not enable that integration, change values or prove service readiness. Clear the filter to restore the full list.

Filters Config Explorer by a field's registered scope. Use it to distinguish corpus-scoped settings from settings shared by the whole backend before editing. Filtering does not move values between scopes or change the active corpus. Inspect the field's effective value and owner when determining which configuration a save will affect.

Filters Config Explorer by the field's registered change-impact category, such as live use, reindexing or redeployment. Use it to find settings that need coordinated operational work after saving. The category is metadata, not proof the required operation has completed. Verify the actual consumer and deployment before attributing a behavior change to the saved value.

Filters Config Explorer by the field's registered product surface, such as runtime or training. It helps locate settings associated with the workflow being inspected. It changes only the list shown and does not switch services, alter field scope or enable a feature. A registered surface may include configuration whose active consumer still needs verification.

Selects the configuration section displayed in the raw configuration view. Use it to inspect the underlying structured values for one domain without scanning the entire document. Selecting a section does not save changes or change the active corpus. When editing raw values, retain the typed field constraints and use the view's explicit save action to persist valid configuration.

Displays the latest recorded query trace, optionally scoped to the selected corpus. The viewer loads the stored trace and presents available routing, retrieval, reranker and gating events, route metadata and external observability links. It does not replay the query or prove a new run occurred. A missing event is not proof that a stage succeeded; use recorded errors and provenance to interpret the pipeline. Set an enabled tracing mode and run a real query before refreshing when no trace exists.

Stored maximum code-snippet length for semantic chunk summaries, default 2,000 characters, range 500 to 10,000. The current deterministic Data Quality builder does not read this field or attach a capped code snippet, so changing it does not shorten stored chunk text or reduce model context. It is distinct from the purpose and identifier limits that the builder does consume. Inspect actual summary fields when assessing coverage, and use chunking or hydration controls for the text shown to retrieval and generation.

Stored maximum API routes per chunk summary, default 5, range 1 to 20. The current deterministic Data Quality summary builder returns an empty routes list and does not consume this field; raising it does not discover additional endpoints. It is separate from the identifier limit, which is used to extract symbols. A useful route list would need an extraction consumer before this knob could control its coverage. Review the generated summaries instead of treating the stored maximum as an observed route count.

Maximum unique identifier tokens the deterministic Data Quality builder records in each summary. Default 5, range 1 to 20. Tokens are scanned from chunk text in appearance order; they are lightweight identifiers rather than a full semantic symbol table. With enrichment enabled, the same list supplies technical details and domain concepts. A larger cap preserves more names at the cost of noisier metadata; a small cap can miss a useful name appearing later. Rebuild summaries after changing it and inspect representative chunks.

Maximum characters in the deterministic summary purpose field. Default 240, range 50 to 500. The builder uses a detected definition name or the first suitable nonempty source line and truncates long purpose text with an ellipsis. This is display and metadata text, not a model-generated explanation or a cap on the original chunk. A shorter purpose is easier to scan but can cut off needed qualifiers; a longer one preserves more source wording. Rebuild summaries and inspect examples after changing it.

Stored list of quick-tip strings, empty by default, intended by the schema for the summary builder UI. The current UI and deterministic builder have no consumer for this field, so editing the list does not display tips or change generated summaries. Values are text guidance rather than retrieval labels or exclusion keywords. Keep that distinction when reviewing configuration: if tips must appear to operators, the consuming surface needs to be wired before this setting has a visible effect.

Literal text prepended to inputs before embedding, empty by default. The embedder concatenates prefix, input text and suffix without inserting separators, so include any needed space or newline in the value. For example, a model-required document instruction must have the exact formatting expected by that model. Added text uses the same token budget and can affect truncation. Prefix and suffix are recorded in the dense embedding contract; changing them on an indexed corpus requires a matching reindex so query and stored embeddings remain compatible.

Literal text appended to inputs before embedding, empty by default. It is joined directly after the input, with no automatic newline or space. Use it only for a deliberate model input format; irrelevant repeated text can shift embeddings and consume token room. Because prefix, input and suffix are assembled before truncation, the configured truncation mode can remove text from the resulting sequence. The suffix is part of the recorded dense contract, so a change requires reindexing existing vectors under the same new configuration.

Stored minimum chunk length for code enrichment, default 50 characters, range 10 to 500. The current deterministic Data Quality summary path does not use this threshold and no active enrichment implementation consumes it. Changing it therefore does not currently filter which summaries are built. The working summary filters are directory, file-pattern and content-keyword exclusions. Treat this as an inactive enrichment setting until a consumer exists, and verify actual builder results instead of inferring behavior from the saved value.

Stored maximum characters for a code enrichment prompt, default 1,000, range 100 to 5,000. No active enrichment request uses this field in the current implementation; the Data Quality summary builder is deterministic and does not call an LLM. Increasing it does not currently expand a model context or incur gateway work. For real text-budget changes, inspect the chunking and retrieval hydration controls. This field needs an enrichment consumer before its intended prompt-size tradeoff can be measured.

Stored timeout for a code enrichment call, default 30 seconds, range 5 to 120. There is currently no active enrichment-call consumer for this field, so changing it does not control deterministic summary-build timing or graph extraction calls. Semantic graph extraction and figure descriptions have their own explicit timeout settings. Keep timeout scopes distinct when diagnosing slow indexing: use the run events to identify the lane before tuning a setting. An enrichment implementation would need wiring before this saved timeout has a runtime effect.

Stored default eval dataset file path, data/evaluation_dataset.json. Current corpus-scoped dataset CRUD and evaluation load data/eval_datasets/<corpus_id>.json instead; changing this config field does not redirect those active corpus dataset routes. Use the Eval Dataset surface to inspect and edit the dataset that the selected corpus actually evaluates. A path is an artifact location, not a guarantee that data was loaded or that entries have valid expected paths and answers. Check dataset identity and entry counts before comparing runs.

Maximum output tokens for Ragas judge calls and the Promptfoo llm-rubric grader. Default 4,096, range 256 to 16,000. This is independent of chat.max_tokens: structured faithfulness statements and reasoning-capable graders can need more output space than the answer being tested. A small budget can truncate the verdict and fail a run; a larger budget permits more paid output without proving a better judgment. Inspect judge failures and representative outputs, then allow enough room for a complete verdict while keeping model and rubric fixed for comparisons.

Rank cutoff used for the result field named precision_at_5. Default 5, range 1 to 200. Ragweld counts matching retrieved chunks within the first K positions and divides by K; repeated chunks matching the same expected file can count as relevant positions. With two matching chunks among the first five, precision is 0.40. Recall and NDCG instead track newly satisfied expectations, so those metrics can tell a different story. Changing K changes precision even though its field name stays precision_at_5. Record cutoffs, dataset and corpus identity when comparing runs.

Rank cutoff used for the result field named recall_at_5. Default 5, range 1 to 200. Ragweld counts distinct expected files or locations satisfied within the first K retrieved chunks and divides by the number of expected items; repeated chunks from one expectation do not inflate recall. For example, finding two of four expectations yields 0.50. A larger cutoff permits a wider candidate window and can increase recall while requiring more retrieval work. The output field name stays recall_at_5 even after changing its cutoff, so record the configured K when comparing runs.

Rank cutoff used for the result field named recall_at_10. Default 10, range 1 to 200. Ragweld counts distinct expected files or locations satisfied within the first K retrieved chunks and divides by the number of expected items; repeated chunks from one expectation do not inflate recall. For example, finding two of four expectations yields 0.50. A larger cutoff permits a wider candidate window and can increase recall while requiring more retrieval work. The output field name stays recall_at_10 even after changing its cutoff, so record the configured K when comparing runs.

Rank cutoff used for the result field named recall_at_20. Default 20, range 1 to 200. Ragweld counts distinct expected files or locations satisfied within the first K retrieved chunks and divides by the number of expected items; repeated chunks from one expectation do not inflate recall. For example, finding two of four expectations yields 0.50. A larger cutoff permits a wider candidate window and can increase recall while requiring more retrieval work. The output field name stays recall_at_20 even after changing its cutoff, so record the configured K when comparing runs.

Rank cutoff used for the result field named ndcg_at_10. Default 10, range 1 to 200. Ragweld rewards the first occurrence of each satisfied expectation with a logarithmic rank discount, then normalizes against an ideal ordering of those expectations. Finding relevant evidence earlier improves the score; repeating the same relevant file does not add new gain. Larger K evaluates a broader tail and may require more results. The metric field name remains ndcg_at_10 when K changes, so keep cutoff, expected paths and corpus versions fixed for meaningful comparisons.

Adds generation-quality scoring with Ragas to evaluation runs. Default false. When enabled, each eval entry is answered through the LiteLLM gateway and scored with the configured judge and selected metrics, instead of assessing only retrieval hit positions. Faithfulness checks supported claims against retrieved context, while answer relevancy measures how well the answer addresses the question. This adds generation and judge calls, latency and spend; a required judge failure fails the eval run rather than returning skipped scores. Enable it when answer behavior matters, and compare runs with a stable judge and metric selection.

LiteLLM alias used to score Ragas metrics. Empty by default, which selects the configured chat default alias. The judge must support the structured responses needed by the metric; its identity is separate from the answer-generation behavior under test. A stronger judge may handle nuanced support better but increases cost and can change score calibration. Use a stable alias for before/after comparisons and review a few verdicts against source evidence. Gateway resolution and judge failures fail scoring; an empty value is explicit default selection, not a promise that an unavailable model is replaced.

Seconds allowed per Ragas judge request through LiteLLM. Default 600, range 30 to 3,600. Slow local serving can need several minutes; too short a limit fails otherwise valid scoring, while a generous limit waits longer before exposing a stalled request. The Ragas runner serializes judge work and disables its own retries; this is not the total duration limit for a multi-entry eval. A timeout fails the eval run rather than silently omitting metrics. Diagnose model latency and judge output size before increasing the limit.

Metrics computed when Ragas evaluation is enabled. Defaults to faithfulness and answer_relevancy, the two supported names; an empty or unsupported selection fails readiness. Faithfulness evaluates whether answer claims are supported by retrieved context. Answer relevancy evaluates how well the response addresses the question and uses embeddings in addition to judge generation. These measure different properties, so a relevant answer can still be unsupported and a supported answer can miss the question. Selecting more metrics adds work. Record metric selection and judge identity when comparing runs.

LiteLLM model alias used for Promptfoo llm-rubric assertions. Empty by default, which uses the answer provider resolved from the chat default alias. Each eligible eval entry supplies its expected answer as the rubric; the grader judges the generated response against that text. Changing the grader can change pass rates without a retrieval or answer-model improvement. Keep it stable across regression comparisons, inspect failed examples and use clear expected answers. The evaluation judge output budget controls grader output independently of the tested answer budget.

Account used to authenticate graph storage connections, default neo4j. The password comes from the operator secret NEO4J_PASSWORD rather than this text field. The account needs the graph operations required by indexing and retrieval; per-corpus database creation additionally requires administrative privileges when automatic creation is enabled. A valid username does not establish readiness by itself: the target URI, password and resolved database must also work. Keep service identity and permissions deliberate, and use readiness details to distinguish authentication failure from a missing database.

Database name used in shared mode, default neo4j. Corpus graph records share that database but retain corpus/generation scope in their data; the name does not select which corpus is active in the UI. In per_corpus mode, a corpus id and configured prefix determine the database instead. A wrong name can make graph reads or indexing fail even when the server is reachable. Confirm the selected Neo4j edition and database readiness before changing isolation strategy, and do not expect a name change to migrate existing graph data.

Selects shared or per_corpus database routing, default shared. Shared uses the configured neo4j_database and is compatible with Neo4j Community, which supports one standard database plus the system database. Per_corpus derives a separate database name from the corpus id and prefix and requires Enterprise multi-database support. Separate databases isolate graph storage more strongly but require provisioning and permissions. Switching this setting changes where clients look; it does not migrate existing graphs. Verify databases and reindex deliberately when changing storage routing.

Prefix used to derive database names in per_corpus mode, default tribrid_. Ragweld appends the corpus id, lowercases and sanitizes the result to alphanumeric/underscore characters, collapses repeated underscores and limits the name to 63 characters. A leading digit receives db_. For example, a corpus id with punctuation can resolve to a normalized name rather than its raw label. It has no routing effect in shared mode. Changing the prefix changes the target database, not the existing graph location, so plan provisioning and reindexing first.

Whether corpus creation attempts to create a missing Neo4j database when per_corpus routing is selected. Default true. This needs Enterprise multi-database support and an account permitted to create databases; it has no per-corpus creation effect in shared mode. Disable it when an operator provisions databases separately. Automatic creation establishes the database container, not indexed entities, relationships or retrieval quality. Verify the resolved database and indexing completion afterward; readiness can still fail when the database cannot be reached or credentials lack the needed access.

Widest relative uncertainty band allowed for a published point estimate of indexing work. Default 0.9, greater than zero and at most 1.0. The band comes from measured variation in tokens per byte, not simply the percentage of corpus bytes sampled. A lower limit requires a tighter estimate and can delay consent while more measurement is needed; a higher limit accepts broader uncertainty. It does not cap the actual indexing bill or guarantee a runtime duration. Read the measured coverage and cost band before approving a run.

Number of files that must be measured in every present format group before the index estimate may publish a point estimate. Default 1, range 1 to 1,000. A corpus containing PDFs and text needs measurements for both groups so an unmeasured format is not silently omitted. Raising the floor improves coverage but can require more extraction work and estimate time, particularly with many formats. It is a sample-coverage condition, not the number of documents indexed. Use it with the relative-error limit and inspect any unavailable-estimate explanation.

Optional tokens-per-second override used to estimate local embedding duration. Unset by default; when provided, the schema requires an integer from 100 to 500,000. It is planning input, not a throttle on actual embedding execution. A value measured with a different model, machine or batching regime can make the estimate misleading; measure representative throughput on the actual runtime before setting it. Faster declared throughput shortens the forecast without making a run faster, so assess estimated ranges alongside real completed-run duration.

Seconds between checks for changed learning-reranker adapter artifacts, default 60, range 10 to 600. This applies to the learning model path when reload-on-change is enabled; it does not schedule training or affect cloud reranker calls. A shorter interval can pick up a published adapter sooner but checks files more often. A longer interval reduces that work and can delay adoption until a later inference request triggers a check. Confirm the configured mode and loaded artifact identity when diagnosing why a newly trained adapter is not yet active.

Question that the evaluation runner sends to retrieval and, when configured, answer generation. Write it as a real user could ask it without seeing the source document, with enough names or conditions to identify the intended subject. Expected paths and optional locations label relevant evidence; an expected answer supplies the generation-grading rubric. For example, ask how often a named sensor is calibrated rather than asking what this document says. Rephrasing the question changes the test, so keep dataset versions stable when comparing retrieval settings.

Written justification for retrying an eligible semantic indexing run whose complete approved extraction succeeded but produced no graph. The reason needs at least 20 visible characters and the authenticated proxy must supply operator identity. The retry records identity, reason, timestamp and telemetry and promotes complete chunks and vectors while graph retrieval remains disabled. It does not bypass failed extraction or arbitrary graph invariants; if the graph already passes, remove the override and retry normally. Explain why the reviewed corpus is intentionally entity sparse so later operators can audit the decision.

Graph viewer state labelled Max hops, initially 2, range 1 to 5. A hop means crossing one relationship from a seed entity. In the current viewer store this value is saved in session state but is not sent by graph-load, subgraph or entity-selection requests, so editing it does not currently change the fetched neighborhood. It is distinct from graph_search.max_hops, which the retrieval leg actually consumes. Use the displayed neighborhood and request results to assess graph coverage rather than inferring depth from this inactive viewer control.

Stored graph_storage.max_hops setting, default 2, range 1 to 5. The active retrieval traversal reads graph_search.max_hops instead, so changing this storage-section value does not currently alter retrieval depth. A graph hop crosses one relationship from a seed; deeper active traversal can find longer dependency chains but increases branching and candidate work. Use the Graph Search setting for that measured tradeoff, and keep it distinct from the graph viewer display state. Inspect trace parameters before interpreting a saved storage limit as executed depth.

Stored graph_storage.graph_search_top_k value, default 30, range 5 to 100. The active graph retrieval leg uses graph_search.top_k rather than this storage-section field, so changing it does not currently increase returned candidates. Top-k normally means a bounded number of ranked results, with higher active values trading more evidence for more downstream work. Tune the consumed Graph Search top-k control and inspect leg counts in actual results. Do not infer retrieval coverage from this duplicate stored setting.

Stored list of entity types, initially function, class, module, variable and import. The current code graph derives parsed node kinds and the semantic graph uses its approved schema; neither extraction path reads graph_storage.entity_types. Editing this list therefore does not change what current indexing extracts. It is also separate from viewer type filters, which hide loaded entities locally. Review the approved semantic schema or code-graph policy when changing extraction vocabulary, then reindex and inspect the actual type breakdown.

Stored list of relationship labels, initially calls, imports, inherits, contains and references. The current code graph writes its parsed relationship kinds and the semantic pipeline follows an approved schema; this storage list is not consumed by those extraction paths. Changing it does not currently add, remove or filter indexed edges. Viewer relationship checkboxes instead filter the local display. For a real extraction change, review the schema or code-graph policy and inspect a new indexed generation before attributing changed retrieval to this saved list.

Whether the indexing run performs graph community construction after graph promotion, default true at graph_storage.include_communities. This controls graph analysis work and readiness expectations; it is separate from graph_search.include_communities, which enables query-time community expansion. Building communities can support broad subsystem context but adds indexing work, and useful communities depend on actual graph structure. Turning query-time expansion on does not create absent community data. Inspect community counts and rendered results after indexing before expecting them to improve retrieval.

Stored template describing evidence-based conversational answers. The active chat path uses chat.system_prompt_chat and chat.system_prompt_answer, not system_prompts.main_rag_chat, so editing this template does not currently change chat generation. A useful grounding instruction should tell the model to answer from supplied evidence and acknowledge missing support, but that policy must live in the prompt the route actually consumes. Use the linked chat settings and compare emitted prompt identity before attributing answer changes to this stored template.

Stored template requesting concise alternative search queries with technical synonyms, one per line. The current retrieval implementation has no consumer for system_prompts.query_expansion, so saving revised wording does not currently issue extra searches. Expansion would normally trade wider terminology coverage for more retrieval work and topic drift. Inspect the actual executed query list before assuming this prompt or an expansion toggle changed behavior. Keep semantic meaning fixed in any future variants and evaluate against reviewed questions.

Stored instruction to optimize a search query without changing its meaning. The current search and chat pipeline does not consume system_prompts.query_rewrite, so editing it does not currently rewrite live queries. A real rewrite should preserve named subjects, constraints and negation while clarifying terms; losing a condition can retrieve plausible but wrong evidence. Check executed query traces rather than inferring rewrite behavior from this saved text. The template needs a consumer before its effect can be tested.

Stored JSON-summary template asking for symbols, purpose, technical details, concepts, routes, dependencies and patterns. Current Data Quality and synthetic chunk-summary builders are deterministic and do not call this prompt, so editing it does not currently generate richer model-written summaries. Preserve any required JSON shape if a future consuming implementation uses it. For current behavior, inspect identifier and purpose limits and rebuild the deterministic summaries; do not infer an LLM call or gateway cost from this template being present.

Stored template asking for a concise JSON object with symbols, purpose and keywords. No active code-enrichment implementation consumes system_prompts.code_enrichment in the current pipeline. Editing it therefore does not change indexing metadata or trigger model calls. The deterministic summary builder uses source text and identifiers instead. If you need different current summary coverage, use its filters and output limits. A prompt alone does not establish a runtime feature: verify a consuming request and returned metadata before measuring quality or spend.

Template formatted by the official Neo4j GraphRAG extractor for each semantic chunk. Keep the required {schema} and {text} placeholders; {examples} is optional. The current template defines readable entity names, exact supported relationships, section scope, negation and uncertainty, with JSON-only output. A broad schema permits relationship types but is not evidence that an edge occurred. Editing these instructions changes extraction behavior and can affect graph quality, latency and validity. Review a representative extraction and reindex deliberately rather than assuming existing graph generations use the new prompt.

Instruction used by the evaluation comparison analysis call to explain result differences skeptically. The default asks the model to consider index, dataset and config changes, measurement noise and uncertain causes instead of fabricating a confident explanation. It affects the narrative interpretation, not the underlying retrieval metrics or judge scores. Preserve that distinction when editing tone or structure. A claim that one setting caused an improvement still needs comparable runs and evidence; review the report against recorded config and dataset identities.

Template used for grounded question/answer generation from one source excerpt. The request fills {num_pairs}, {question_max_chars}, {expected_answer_max_chars} and {evidence_quote_max_chars}. Keep these placeholders and the JSON-array fields question, expected_answer and evidence_quote so generated rows match the provider boundary. The default requires self-contained questions and source-only answers with copied evidence. Changing style does not relax subsequent length, grounding and System One checks; malformed or unsupported rows are rejected. Compare kept useful rows and cost on fixed source selection after editing.

System instruction used by the LiteLLM listwise cloud reranker. It scores every candidate passage for direct answer relevance and requires a JSON scores array with one numeric score for each opaque supplied id. Passage text is untrusted data and must not be treated as instructions. The parser requires an exact candidate-id bijection: omissions, unknown ids, duplicates or nonnumeric scores fail reranking. Preserve that contract when editing scoring criteria. Evaluate ordering on reviewed queries; stronger wording cannot compensate for candidates missing from the retrieval pool.

Stored short template asking for symbols, purpose and keywords in JSON. No current deterministic summary or indexing path consumes system_prompts.lightweight_chunk_summaries, so editing it does not make a build faster or change generated summaries. It differs from working summary limits, which directly bound identifier count, purpose length and output coverage. Use those controls for measurable current behavior. Keep the template only as stored configuration until a real consumer exists, and verify actual model requests before assuming a prompt-driven build.

Stored retrieval.hydration_mode value, default lazy, accepting lazy, eager or none (off normalizes to none). No active result-hydration implementation consumes this field, so changing it does not currently alter when source text is loaded or returned. Graph result hydration still follows the graph retrieval implementation, independently of this saved mode. Inspect actual response content and citations when diagnosing missing text; a stored eager value is not proof that full documents were fetched.

Stored retrieval.hydration_max_chars value, default 2,000, range 500 to 10,000. The current retrieval path has no consumer for this field, so editing it does not currently truncate snippets or change generated context length. It is distinct from chunk sizes and from chat answer/context budgeting. A larger saved value does not guarantee more evidence reaches the model; inspect actual returned passages and the consuming generation budget when assessing context coverage.

Stored hydration.hydration_mode value, default lazy, accepting lazy, eager or none (off normalizes to none). No active result-hydration implementation consumes this field, so changing it does not currently alter when source text is loaded or returned. Graph result hydration still follows the graph retrieval implementation, independently of this saved mode. Inspect actual response content and citations when diagnosing missing text; a stored eager value is not proof that full documents were fetched.

Stored hydration.hydration_max_chars value, default 2,000, range 500 to 10,000. The current retrieval path has no consumer for this field, so editing it does not currently truncate snippets or change generated context length. It is distinct from chunk sizes and from chat answer/context budgeting. A larger saved value does not guarantee more evidence reaches the model; inspect actual returned passages and the consuming generation budget when assessing context coverage.

Server-side gate for the benchmark run API. When disabled, new run requests are rejected as benchmarking disabled. Enable it for side-by-side comparisons and separately choose the models and request persistence. This does not start a benchmark automatically or remove previously saved results. Schema default: true.

Stored preference for benchmark cost reporting. The current runner computes model cost metadata without consulting this flag. Changing it does not suppress provider usage or guarantee a different result payload. Use the benchmark's recorded cost fields to compare runs and treat missing provider pricing as a limitation. Schema default: true.

Stored preference for benchmark timing detail. The current runner does not branch on this flag; its measured timing fields remain determined by the execution path. Use timing evidence to identify retrieval versus generation delays, and do not assume toggling this setting removes timing collection. Schema default: true.

Maximum models accepted by the benchmark API and maximum in-flight generation tasks in its runner, constrained to 2–8. Larger limits can compare more models and reduce total elapsed time but increase simultaneous provider load and spend; smaller limits reduce contention. The current frontend separately caps selection at four, so raising this setting above four does not add UI selection capacity. Schema default: 4.

Filesystem directory used for saved benchmark-run JSON and the run-list API. Use a backend-writable location with enough space for results and an appropriate backup policy. Changing it redirects subsequent persistence and listing rather than moving earlier files; keep the path stable when comparing historical runs. Schema default: "data/benchmarks/".

Controls the runner's optional benchmark JSON persistence. Keeping results supports later inspection and comparison; disabling it avoids that runner write. The benchmark API also has an explicit save request path, so this is not a universal prohibition on storing results. Review both the run request and this preference when determining what will persist. Schema default: true.

Corpus IDs initially selected for new conversations. The list is filtered against available registered corpora, and Recall selection also respects its enabled setting. Choose sources that are useful by default without adding unrelated context to every new chat. This seeds new conversation source state; it does not index corpora or overwrite an existing conversation's choices. Schema default: ["recall_default"].

Stored endpoint intended for a future ComfyUI image-generation integration. No active Ragweld consumer submits workflows to this endpoint. An address alone does not install ComfyUI, authenticate requests or identify an executable workflow. Keep it aligned with a future explicitly implemented API path before expecting image output. Schema default: "".

Stored image-output resolution string intended for a future generator. The current schema has no width/height parser or execution consumer enforcing it. Changing the string does not resize attachments or produce images. Use a provider-supported resolution only when a concrete generation path validates and consumes the setting. Schema default: "1024x1024".

Stored image-generation step-count assumption, constrained to 1–50. More steps can increase compute in a supported generator, but Ragweld currently has no image-generation consumer applying this value. It does not alter text generation, training epochs or the number of generated images. Schema default: 8.

Stored image-generation enablement intent. The current source defines and serializes image-generation configuration but has no active image-generation API or UI consumer. Enabling this field does not start an image job or make a generator available. Keep it disabled until a concrete generation integration is implemented and verified. Schema default: false.

Stored command intended for a future local image generator. The schema describes prompt/output/steps/width/height arguments, but no current image-generation execution path invokes it. Changing this string does not run a command, install its package or select chat's text-generation engine. Schema default: "python -m qwen_image.generate".

Stored model path intended for future local image generation. No active image-generation consumer resolves or loads this path. It does not download weights or establish generator readiness. A future integration would need a compatible installed model and a verified backend-reachable filesystem path. Schema default: "".

Stored intended image-generation provider; schema permits local, openai, comfyui_api or replicate. There is currently no execution consumer for this block. Selecting a value neither connects a provider nor launches a job; use it only as configuration intent pending a implemented workflow with explicit credentials and output handling. Schema default: "local".

Stored remote model reference intended for a future Replicate image-generation path. No current execution consumer reads it. Entering a reference does not invoke the model, configure credentials or authorize provider spend. A future integration must validate the model's actual input and output contract. Schema default: "".

Stored preference for an accelerated image-generation adapter. No active image-generation path currently reads it, so toggling it changes configuration only. Adapter compatibility and image quality would need validation in a future implementation; this flag does not prove fewer steps or faster generation. Schema default: true.

Vision-input detail mode, validated as auto, low or high. It is sent with image content to the compatible generation route. Lower detail can reduce image-processing work but may miss small text; high can help detailed document inspection at greater token cost. Provider and model support still govern behavior; this does not change the source image's dimensions. Schema default: "auto".

Maximum allowed size of an uploaded image in megabytes, constrained to 1–50. The composer validates attachments against this limit before sending. A smaller cap reduces request size and browser memory; a larger cap accommodates detailed images but can add processing work. This is an attachment admission limit, not an automatic image-compression control. Schema default: 20.

Maximum number of image attachments accepted for a message, constrained to 1–10. More images can support multi-page comparisons but increase request size and the model's prompt budget. The composer enforces this cap; model vision capability and context limits still apply independently. Schema default: 5.

Image-format names accepted by the chat composer, initially PNG, JPG/JPEG, GIF and WebP. Keep the list limited to formats supported by the actual vision route and attachment handling. Editing the list changes admission checks; it does not add a decoder, animate GIF content or give a text-only model vision capability. Schema default: ["png","jpg","jpeg","gif","webp"].

Optional catalog-backed LiteLLM alias used for image-bearing chat turns. Empty leaves the normal chat route in place when it supports vision. Use a verified vision-capable alias to separate image interpretation from ordinary text chat. An override must still satisfy catalog and provider capability checks; it does not convert an incompatible model into a vision model. Schema default: "".

Stored intended maximum token size for Recall chunks, constrained to 64–1024. The current Recall document builder splits by sentence or by turn and does not read this limit, so lowering it does not split long memory passages. Use the implemented chunking-strategy setting to choose current boundaries; a hard token cap needs an actual consumer before it can be relied on. Schema default: 256.

Selects Recall document boundaries. sentence splits messages at sentence-ending punctuation; the current builder treats other accepted values (paragraph, turn or fixed) as one chunk per nonempty message. Smaller sentence units improve focused memory retrieval but separate context across chunks; turn-sized units preserve message context. This is Recall-specific and does not select code-corpus AST chunking. Schema default: "sentence".

Creation root for Recall corpora, with one subdirectory per corpus ID. Relative paths resolve from the project root; the disposable-lane environment override can replace it. This value is consulted when the corpus is created. Afterwards its registered corpus path is authoritative, so editing this setting does not move an existing Recall corpus or its documents. Schema default: "data/recall".

Stable ID used to identify and create the default Recall corpus. The ID must satisfy corpus-ID path-component validation because it also names a directory. Keep it stable so stored memory remains discoverable; changing it points subsequent Recall setup at a different corpus rather than migrating earlier conversation data. Schema default: "recall_default".

Stored intended embedding-model override for Recall. The current Recall indexer uses the scoped embedding configuration and its recorded corpus contract, without reading this string. Changing it does not re-embed stored memory or replace the active Recall embedding space. Use the actual embedding configuration and indexing contract when changing models. Schema default: "".

Server-side Recall enablement. When disabled, new source initialization removes the default Recall corpus from selected sources and the chat path does not schedule automatic Recall indexing. Enable it for memory continuity and separately control source selection, gating and auto-indexing. This switch is distinct from selecting Recall for a particular conversation. Schema default: true.

Stored experimental intent to add graph indexing and retrieval to Recall. The current Recall indexer does not read this field or build a graph; turning it on does not create Recall graph data. Use existing dense/sparse Recall retrieval, and require an implemented and verified graph path before relying on this setting. Schema default: false.

Stored intended token budget for Recall history, constrained to 512–32768. The current Recall indexer and retrieval path do not read this field, so it does not cap stored conversation text or injected context. Actual context is bounded by retrieval and prompt-budget handling. Do not use this as a memory retention policy. Schema default: 4096.

Stored send-key preference. The current composer uses Ctrl+Enter directly and does not read this string, so changing it does not rebind the shortcut. Use the displayed composer shortcut until a preference consumer is implemented. This field does not change backend chat behavior. Schema default: "ctrl+enter".

Stored preference for source-selector visibility. The current chat interface renders the source dropdown without consulting this flag. Disabling it therefore does not hide sources or prevent retrieval. Conversation source IDs and backend request policy determine what is retrieved. Schema default: true.

Server policy allowing opt-in public-web grounding. This is separate from the conversation's Web checkbox, which starts off. A requested web turn also requires an OpenRouter-backed gateway alias; unsupported routes fail. Disable this policy to block web use at the server boundary, or leave it enabled and let users opt in when current public information is needed. Schema default: true.

OpenRouter web-search engine preference: auto lets the provider select, native requests model-native search, and exa requests that search integration. It is applied only for eligible opt-in web turns. Engine support depends on the upstream model/provider. Changing it does not enable Web for a conversation or provide local corpus retrieval. Schema default: "auto".

Character budget passed to the OpenRouter web-search tool for eligible opt-in turns, constrained to 1000–50000. Larger budgets can provide more source text but increase upstream context work; smaller budgets keep grounding compact and may omit useful detail. Some engines, including native search, ignore this parameter. This is a web-tool budget, not the chat output-token cap or a document indexing limit. Schema default: 12000.

Per-search result limit sent with the web-search request, constrained to 1–20. More results may broaden coverage but add provider work and evidence to inspect; fewer keep results focused. Native search may ignore this budget. This request budget is separate from the total citation count and character budget Ragweld uses when collecting web-grounding metadata. Schema default: 5.

Total web-search result budget passed to OpenRouter for an eligible opt-in web turn, constrained to 1–20. Larger limits can broaden available evidence at greater upstream work and context cost. It is distinct from the per-search result budget and does not guarantee a response contains exactly that many citations. Review returned grounding metadata before claiming web support. Schema default: 5.

Development API port used by runtime diagnostics when BACKEND_PORT does not override it, constrained to 1024–65535. Keep it aligned with the actual listener so diagnostics probe the intended service. Changing the saved field does not rebind a running API or rewrite remote ingress. Schema default: 58012.

Development frontend port used by runtime diagnostics when FRONTEND_PORT does not override it, constrained to 1024–65535. Keep it aligned with the actual frontend listener to avoid diagnosing a different service. Editing it does not move a running listener or deploy an ingress change. Schema default: 55173.

Maximum text/code file size the source viewer will serve in full, constrained to 65536–50000000 bytes. Larger files produce a typed 413 rather than flooding the browser. Raise it only when large source files are necessary for evidence inspection; doing so increases transfer and browser memory. It does not change indexing limits or PDF rendering. Schema default: 5000000.

PDF page raster scale used by the source viewer, constrained to 1–4. One unit is 72 dpi, so scale 2 gives 144 dpi. Higher scales improve small text readability but increase rendering work and bandwidth. It affects viewed page images rather than OCR, extraction or the stored document. Schema default: 2.

PDF citation-thumbnail raster scale, constrained to 0.25–1. A small scale keeps chat citations compact; a larger one makes page context clearer but costs additional render work and transfer. It does not change the full-page viewer scale or captured citation regions. Schema default: 0.5.

Stored switch describing disabled code enrichment. This field is exposed in retrieval configuration, but no current enrichment execution consumer was found reading it. Setting it does not disable indexing, embeddings or chunk-summary generation elsewhere. Verify the actual enrichment implementation before treating this as a workload gate. Schema default: false.

Stored catalog-backed LiteLLM alias for enrichment. It is exposed in model assignments and validated on config writes, but the current indexing enrichment implementation must be checked before attributing generated metadata to this alias. Changing it does not select an embedding model or rewrite existing chunk summaries; inspect the concrete enrichment path and re-run its workload to evaluate effects. Schema default: "ragweld-local".

Output-token cap used by non-chat generation consumers such as evaluation analysis, constrained to 100–16000. Higher budgets support longer analyses but increase potential latency and spend; lower ones can truncate structured or explanatory output. Chat uses its separate chat.max_tokens cap, so editing this field is not a chat response-length control. Schema default: 512.

Catalog-backed LiteLLM alias used by non-chat generation consumers such as evaluation analysis. It is not an upstream provider model ID or a direct-serving endpoint. Chat has its own gateway default. Choose a registered alias and evaluate the relevant task before changing it; the configuration save boundary validates model-policy compatibility. Schema default: "ragweld-local".

Optional stored LiteLLM alias for a CLI-specific generation route. Empty means no override. Current source records this value in model assignments and lineage, but no CLI generation consumer was found applying it. Changing it does not create a CLI route or alter ordinary chat generation; validate a concrete caller before relying on the override. Schema default: "".

Optional stored LiteLLM alias intended for HTTP generation override. Empty means no override. Current source exposes and records the value, but the normal chat provider router does not read it. It does not replace chat.litellm.default_model or directly configure the gateway. Verify a specific endpoint's consumer before attributing behavior to this setting. Schema default: "".

Optional stored LiteLLM alias intended for MCP answer generation. Empty means no override. Current source exposes and records the value, but it is not a model for tool selection or argument construction. Verify the actual MCP answer consumer before relying on this override; changing it does not create provider routes or alter retrieval mode. Schema default: "".

Sampling temperature used by non-chat generation consumers such as evaluation analysis, constrained to 0–2. Lower values reduce variation across repeated grounded analysis; higher values allow more varied phrasing and can increase drift. Tune on representative tasks while keeping model and evidence fixed. Ordinary chat has separate retrieval and direct-chat temperatures. Schema default: 0.

Timeout in seconds used by non-chat generation consumers, including evaluation analysis and synthetic generation, constrained to 10–900. Allow enough time for the configured model and output budget; overly short limits reject valid slow requests, while long limits delay failure reporting. This is independent of chat's streaming timeout. Schema default: 600.

Stored nucleus-sampling preference, constrained to 0–1. Lower values normally narrow token choices in a consumer that sends top_p, but the current non-chat generation consumer does not pass this field to the gateway. Editing it therefore does not prove a sampling change. Chat temperature and actual provider request parameters govern the implemented path. Schema default: 1.

Host-header allowlist used by MCP's DNS-rebinding protection. Localhost and loopback with any port are the initial entries; deployed public hostnames need explicit entries. Wildcard :* allows ports for an otherwise specified hostname. Match the advertised public endpoint without broadly allowing unrelated hosts. This startup-captured transport list requires restart to change the running server. Schema default: ["localhost:*","127.0.0.1:*"].

Origin-header allowlist used by MCP's transport security. Match trusted browser-client origins including scheme, hostname and intended ports; wildcard :* permits varying ports. This is distinct from the Host-header allowlist and is not a general API CORS setting. Keep it narrow and restart after editing because the MCP server captures the list at construction. Schema default: ["http://localhost:*","http://127.0.0.1:*"].

Retrieval mode used when an MCP caller omits mode: tribrid combines the configured lanes; dense_only, sparse_only and graph_only select one lane. Explicit tool mode takes precedence, and the selected lane still requires compatible indexed data. The mounted tools capture this default at server construction, so restart after changing it. Schema default: "tribrid".

Result count used by MCP search and answer tools when the caller omits top_k, constrained to 1–200. Larger values broaden retrieved evidence and work; smaller values keep results focused. Explicit tool arguments take precedence. The mounted tools capture this default when the server is built, so saved edits require restart before they affect calls. Schema default: 20.

Enables MCP transport checks against allowed Host and Origin values. Keep it enabled and configure the actual deployed hostname and client origins explicitly. Disabling it removes those transport checks rather than solving a mismatched public URL. The server captures this policy at construction, so restart after changing it and verify both allowed and rejected requests. Schema default: true.

Controls whether the embedded MCP Streamable HTTP app is mounted when the API process starts. Enable it for external MCP clients or disable it when the endpoint is not needed. The mounted state is captured at startup, so saving a different value does not hot-mount or unmount the running transport; restart and verify the advertised endpoint. Schema default: true.

Requests JSON responses from the MCP Streamable HTTP server rather than its alternative streaming response behavior. Keep it enabled for the recommended stateless setup unless a verified client requires a different transport response. This is server-construction configuration and takes effect after restart, not immediately when saved. Schema default: true.

Path prefix where the embedded MCP transport is mounted at API startup. It must contain at least one nonempty path segment; the bare root path is invalid. Coordinate it with the advertised public URL and reverse proxy. Changing the stored path needs a process restart; clients must then use the newly mounted endpoint. Schema default: "/mcp".

Client-reachable API origin used to advertise the MCP endpoint, with the configured mount path appended exactly once. Use the public proxy hostname rather than an internal service address when clients connect remotely. Its Host value must also be allowed by DNS-rebinding protection; otherwise an advertised reachable URL can still receive HTTP 421. This field changes advertised navigation, not listener binding. Schema default: "http://127.0.0.1:58012".

Requires Authorization: Bearer with the backend environment's MCP_API_KEY on inbound MCP HTTP requests. Enabling it with no configured secret fails server construction rather than publishing an unprotected endpoint. The credential stays outside this public config. Change the startup policy and environment coherently, restart, and verify authenticated client access. Schema default: false.

Selects stateless MCP HTTP behavior when the process-wide FastMCP server is constructed. Enabled suits independently handled requests without persistent transport sessions. Client compatibility and server behavior depend on the SDK's transport semantics. Saving a change does not rebuild the already-created server; restart before testing clients against the new mode. Schema default: true.

Stored preference to include alert-resolution notifications. The current observability status and incident path does not read this flag as an outbound notification gate. Alertmanager delivery is configured in the observability infrastructure. Changing this field alone does not alter Alertmanager routing or send messages. Schema default: true.

Stored comma-separated severity preference for alert notifications. The current notification path does not consume it; actual Alertmanager routing controls delivery. Changing this string does not suppress incidents in the operator view or configure receivers. Keep intended severities aligned with the infrastructure's rules and verify the concrete delivery route. Schema default: "critical,warning".

Stored outbound-alert timeout preference, in seconds. No current outbound webhook consumer was found reading it. Actual notification delivery timeouts belong to the configured Alertmanager receivers. Increasing this value does not repair delivery or alter the API's observability readiness probe timeout. Schema default: 5.

Backend-reachable Langfuse endpoint used to initialize generation observations and check observability readiness. Use the private ingest/API address reachable from the Ragweld process; configure the public URL separately for browser links. A configured address alone does not establish credentials, project access or enabled observation. Verify functional readiness after changing it. Schema default: "".

Stored logging-level preference. Current logging setup is initialized independently and no runtime consumer was found applying this field. Editing it does not necessarily reconfigure active logger levels. Use the actual process logging configuration for DEBUG/INFO/WARNING changes and verify resulting logs. Schema default: "INFO".

Stored metrics enablement preference. The current metric registration and request instrumentation do not consult this field as a master switch. Disabling it therefore does not guarantee metrics stop being collected or exposed. Verify actual instrumentation and scraping when controlling telemetry volume. Schema default: true.

Maximum number of local workbench traces retained per corpus, not a duration. More records provide a longer recent investigation history at greater storage and UI cost; fewer discard old evidence sooner. Eviction is count-based in the trace store. External Tempo, Loki and other backends have separate retention configuration. Schema default: 50.

Optional JSON file used to persist the local workbench trace store. Empty keeps this store in memory only. Choose a backend-writable stable location to retain trace evidence across process restarts; a filesystem path does not replace external OTel export or its retention policy. Capacity remains bounded by the configured trace-count retention. Schema default: "".

Selects auto or mlx_qwen3 for the learning reranker's implemented MLX Qwen3 engine. auto resolves supported hardware; mlx_qwen3 explicitly selects that engine. Unsupported old backend names fail schema validation rather than activating another stack. Verify hardware and artifact compatibility before training or selecting learning-mode inference. Schema default: "auto".

Minimum primary-metric improvement needed for automatic learning-reranker promotion, constrained to 0–1. Increase it to reduce switches caused by small noisy gains; lower it to accept smaller measured improvements. It is an absolute metric-delta threshold rather than a significance test. Keep the comparison dataset and primary goal consistent when interpreting a candidate gain. Schema default: 0.

MLX base checkpoint used for Learning Agent LoRA training. Existing adapters retain base-model identity and artifacts trained against another base are not promotable. Change this only when deliberately retraining from a different compatible base; it does not change the local text-serving model or LiteLLM chat alias. Record base identity with the run to interpret comparisons. Schema default: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit".

Number of training micro-batches accumulated before one MLX optimizer update, constrained to 1–128. Increasing it raises effective batch size without an equally large individual batch, at the cost of fewer updates per processed example. Tune it with batch size and learning rate; this local MLX trainer does not imply distributed world-size multiplication. Schema default: 8.

Minimum evaluation-loss decrease required for automatic Learning Agent promotion: baseline_loss minus new_loss must be at least epsilon. The schema accepts 0–10. Increase it to avoid promotion on small noisy gains; reduce it to accept smaller decreases. Promotion changes the training-only active adapter baseline and lineage, not the LiteLLM chat-serving model. Schema default: 0.

Gates automatic promotion of a completed Learning Agent adapter on evaluation-loss improvement. When enabled, the loss decrease must satisfy the configured epsilon; disabling the gate permits promotion after a successful run without that comparison. The promoted store remains a training-only baseline for subsequent runs and lineage, not a live chat deployment. Schema default: true.

Optimizer-step interval between Learning Agent trainer telemetry events, constrained to 1–20. First and final events are emitted as well. A shorter interval gives denser loss and optimization curves but adds event traffic; a longer interval reduces overhead and can miss brief changes. It controls training telemetry, not agent tool-use logging or model serving. Schema default: 2.

Optional dataset path for Learning Agent training. Empty uses the configured evaluation dataset path. Choose the intended backend-readable dataset and record its version with the run so comparisons use the same supervision. This is the Learning Agent dataset input, separate from reranker's triplet path, and changing it does not generate data. Schema default: "".
